### The category in one weight

Write $E$ for a unital spaces operad for little $n$-discs, and $F$ for its free algebra functor. The $n$-fold hom of the raw presentation is the $E$-monoidal infinity-category freely adjoining the declared arrows to the free $E$-space of configurations on the colours. Indeed a map from the delooping chooses those colours and an arrow at each of the two specified configurations in the target iterated hom. This is the cellular mapping property at the actual attaching faces. As in Responses 36 and 38 we can use ordinary infinity-categories here since all higher cells are groupoidal. Moving the attaching configurations along paths gives the equivalent presentation with the attaching arrows transported at their two ends. Use the point-boundary transport there if the scalar faces have nonstandard writings. [Scalar realization](#researcher-response-36) · [Directed attachments at configurations](#researcher-response-38)

Here is an explicit presentation before categorical realization. For colour set $C$ and rule set $J$, in simplicial spaces form the pushout of $F(C)$ and $F(J\times\Delta^1)$ over $F(J\times\partial\Delta^1)$ using the two attaching maps. In simplicial degree $q$ the result is
$$
                  F\big(C\amalg(J\times\{1,\ldots,q\})\big).
$$
Indeed the constant endpoints of $\Delta^1_q$ are separate free generators from its $q$ nonconstant simplices. The pushout simply adjoins the latter, also for the derived pushout by the free coproduct mapping property. An outer face that discards the jump of a nonconstant simplex substitutes its prescribed endpoint configuration. Other face and degeneracy maps retain the jump with its induced index. Categorical realization sends $\Delta^1$ to the directed interval and constant spaces to groupoids. It preserves products and is left adjoint to the complete Segal nerve, hence induces the same adjunction on $E$-algebras; on free algebras it commutes with $F$. Thus the levelwise presentation realizes to exactly the algebra just described. Its underlying simplicial space splits by total weight, and realization preserves this coproduct. [Rezk, Theorems 7.2 and 7.7](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9811037) · [Free operadic algebra formula](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/papers/HA.pdf#page=346)

In weight $L<2W$ a configuration in any simplicial degree contains at most one jump. The no-jump part $G$ is the pure configuration groupoid of weight $L$. For each rule $j$ and multiset of stationary colours of complementary weight, let $V$ be the configuration space on those colours and one distinguished site. There are maps $a,b:V\to G$ inserting the two attaching configurations there. Consequently the weight component is obtained from $G$ by adjoining the cylinders $V\times[1]$ at these maps. This follows levelwise from the displayed formula, including the two endpoint faces. Quotients for repeated stationary colours are the usual free permutation quotients. The cylinders are attached in infinity-categories, so the arrows retain their direction.

For fixed objects $x,y$, the mapping space is a coproduct over finite ordered lists of cylinders of the following spaces. Pick $z_i\in V_i$ for each use. Supply paths in the pure groupoid
$$
 x\leadsto a_1z_1,\qquad b_i z_i\leadsto a_{i+1}z_{i+1},\qquad b_d z_d\leadsto y.                 \tag{16}
$$
For an empty list take the ordinary path space. One verification is by the free category enriched in spaces under the groupoid $G$. The bimodule of a single adjoined family from $x$ to $y$ is the homotopy sum over $V$ of $G(x,az)\times G(bz,y)$. By Yoneda, a map from this bimodule into the homs of a target under $G$ is precisely a family of arrows at $(az,bz)$ natural on $V$. Take the tensor algebra of these bimodules under relative tensor over $G$, with the homs of $G$ as unit. It has the free extension mapping property. In the $d$-th tensor power each intermediate coend composes two representables to $G(b_i z_i,a_{i+1}z_{i+1})$, giving (16). This also explains why the different visits to a rule have separate configuration parameters even for a loop rule. [Enriched free categories and relative composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.3881)

### Reading the old boundary and constructing its projections

Use the state and copy algebras of Response 38. At each output port the state now records the whole tuple of input states, the rule and that port's index. These are functions with several outputs of exactly the kind verified there. Include a copied rule for each ordered input tuple with these prescribed outputs. Once the initial particles have distinct leaf names, a surface witness and its old faces therefore lift together, with their literal old heads. Starting at the final names and tracing their records recovers all uses: every use has an output, and a consumed output occurs in the next record that uses it. In a strict representative one can read the uses chronologically by sequentializing the ordinary strict paste, with unchanged wires at each use. At every stage the live names are distinct. A record cannot be created twice: its ordered nonempty tuple would have to be consumed twice; the initial names occur once and this argument inducts on record depth. All output records of one use refer to that same use.

Consecutive uses have a wire in common in the intermediate configuration: otherwise their output and input groups would have disjoint weights each exceeding $L/2$. Hence their dependence order is total. In particular the lifted end names determine their order, all ports, and the wires that remain stationary at every step. The argument also applies with no uses. We may restrict to the finite computad of just these wire names and these copied declarations. The closed strict support of the lifted boundary is contained there. Indeed its $(n+1)$-paste consists of these events with their intervening wires, and above that rank its strict value is an iterated identity. If there are two boundary arrows, the compatible state lift gives the same final names and therefore the same events. Support restriction in Response 27 applies to raw terms and to a proposed surface filler above rank $n+1$, whose strict value has the same support. Folding a raw filler from this finite computad returns the requested raw term. At degree $n+1$ itself a surface arrow gives an ordinary strict rewrite history. Each change there has a raw representative by placing the rule beside the specified stationary particles and fitting at the two pure configurations by paths. Composing these representatives fits at the old ends. In lower degrees only the scalar skeleton is needed. [State lifting for arbitrary functions](#researcher-response-38) · [Closed support restriction](#researcher-response-27)

Write $P_j$ for the set of live wires after $j$ uses, $X_j$ for its ordered configuration space, and $V_i$ now for the ordered configuration of the stationary wires and the distinguished site of use $i$. Each name at these profiles appears once. In (16) the two incident maps of use $i$ are $a_i:V_i\to X_{i-1}$ and $b_i:V_i\to X_i$. Each admits a homotopy retraction: keep one specified input or output, respectively, and the stationary names. The residual unary disc operation is homotopic to the unit. In the named computad the old boundaries under consideration belong to this one summand, as the support and endpoint reconstruction show.

For each cut $j$ there is a **raw substitution to the pure scalars named by $P_j$**. Send the wires present at this cut to their singleton names. Proceed backwards through earlier uses and forwards through later ones. Keep the stationary assignments. In the backwards direction assign the entire multiset on the outputs to one input, and the empty multiset to the other inputs; forwards concentrate the inputs onto one output. A wire retains its assignment for its whole lifetime. Use scalar composites for these multisets, and iterated identities for empty ones. At each copied rule the two images use the same multiset, so they admit a raw connecting arrow by connectivity of the pure configuration component and the prescribed-boundary test. Choose one such arrow. This defines a substitution on the actual presentation; in particular it also translates any surface witness.

On pure configurations of any $P_i$ the substitution operates by insertion of the assigned blocks at their sites. This follows from the free $E$-algebra mapping property on the pure part. At $i=j$ it induces the identity. At $i<j$ this map factors up to homotopy through $b_j:V_j\to X_j$. At the last step before $j$ keep the one selected input and all stationary names, then insert the output block. Earlier concentrations compose with this one by operad substitution. Any fixed choices of ordering or composite for these *named* blocks give homotopic maps, by path connectivity of the corresponding ordered configuration spaces. The dual factorization holds for $i>j$ through $a_{j+1}$. The substitutions on (16) concatenate the resulting paths with the chosen rule images at their sites, by functoriality. In a fibre in which all $z_i$ are fixed these rule paths are fixed translations.

### Why the substitutions detect higher fillers

For $n\ge3$ all the ordered configuration spaces above are simply connected, including the empty and singleton cases. The space (16) projects by a path fibration to $\prod V_i$, with fibre a product of paths in the $X_j$ at specified ends. It is connected. On homotopy groups the connecting map for $t\ge2$ is the incidence homomorphism
$$
 D_t:\bigoplus_{i=1}^d\pi_t V_i\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=0}^d\pi_t X_j,
 \qquad v_i\longmapsto (\ldots,(a_i)_*v_i,-(b_i)_*v_i,\ldots).
$$
This is the two-endpoint path fibration, pulled back for each path in (16); a choice of opposite orientations changes all signs together. Paths for changes of basepoint are immaterial by simple connectivity. The first coordinate forces $v_1=0$ in the kernel, and induction forces every $v_i=0$, since every $(a_i)_*$ is injective. The long exact sequence therefore identifies $\pi_{t-1}$ of (16) with $\operatorname{coker}D_t$, also for $t=2$ since $\pi_1\prod V_i=0$.

The cut substitutions jointly inject this cokernel into $\prod_j\pi_t X_j$. To see this, represent a class by $(u_0,\ldots,u_d)$. Its $j$-th test adds the images of the $u_i$ under the pure configuration maps just calculated: on the fixed fibre this is concatenation of loops and fixed paths. Cellular substitution defines it on the total space, so it vanishes on the incidence relations. Suppose every test vanishes. In the last test all terms except $u_d$ belong to the image of $(b_d)_*$, and $u_d$ has coefficient the identity. Eliminate $u_d$ by an incidence relation. Now use the $(d-1)$-st test, in which all later entries have become zero, and continue to the zeroth test. There the sole remaining entry vanishes. This proves injectivity integrally on every homotopy group, without requiring a homology test to detect homotopy.

In particular the named summand is $(n-3)$-connected. If $p_j$ is the size of $P_j$ and $v_i$ is one plus the number of stationary wires at use $i$, its $\pi_{n-2}$ is free abelian of rank
$$
                 \sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom{p_j}{2}-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\binom{v_i}{2}.
$$
Indeed ordered configurations are $(n-2)$-connected and their $\pi_{n-1}$ is freely generated in pair coordinates. The incidence map is injective, and the joint cut test embeds its cokernel in a free abelian group. This computes an obstruction at the old boundary with each intermediate configuration counted, even when there are stationary wires. [Integral pair coordinates](#researcher-response-47)

At degree $n+2$ connectivity supplies the desired comparison of the two lifted arrows. At greater degree the prescribed parallel globes bound exactly when their glued sphere is null in this mapping space, by the fixed-hom globe test. Every cut substitution takes the old globes and the proposed surface filler to its pure scalar context. Pure conservativity supplies a raw filler there, so each test of the sphere vanishes. The joint injection gives a raw filler at the original boundary after folding. Pure conservativity for binary $\{A,U\}$ and published insertion is Response 59. [Pure scalar theorem](#researcher-response-59) · [Returning a filler at prescribed faces](#researcher-response-36)

For $n=2$ the ordered configuration spaces are aspherical. Every component of (16) has zero higher homotopy: its fibre over $\prod V_i$ is homotopy discrete, and the stabilizer in $\prod\pi_1V_i$ of any component of the fibre is trivial. Indeed the first end path forces $(a_1)_*v_1=1$ by cancellation in the fundamental groupoid; the next forces $(a_2)_*v_2=1$, and so on. The same retractions give injectivity. This settles all degrees from five onwards at the lifted boundary, and Response 5 handles the lower degrees in the original context for all ten surfaces. [Planar configuration calculation](#researcher-response-36) · [Degree-four comparison](#researcher-response-5)

Finally, for the criterion without initial weights, lift the old data to occurrences and restrict to their finite supported presentation as above. Total dependence is now the hypothesis. Every wire lies on an initial-to-final path since all rules have positive inputs and outputs. Send one unit of flow along a finite list of such paths covering all wires. In a finite totally ordered dependence graph, each consecutive pair of events shares a wire: a longer directed path between them would have another event strictly between. Hence there is one initial-to-final path traversing every event. Add more units along this path than the entire previous initial flow. Wire flows are positive integer weights, preserved at every rule, and every rule now uses more than half the total. Apply the weight result in this supported computad. If there are no events, support already restricts to the pure case. Incomparable events can give simplices containing several jumps in the same configuration; their contribution to the unrestricted classification in Q1 is still open. ∎

On three consecutive uses its pair-coordinate matrices had 13 input coordinates, an incidence image of rank two and joint probe rank eleven, with zero composite. In simplicial degree three it found 30 one-jump profiles below weight twelve and 21 two-jump profiles at twelve. ## Researcher Response 79

**The finite history groups in Response 77 embed effectively into the ordinary braid group.** For any finite Gray 2-computad, fix two temporal histories $H,J$ of equal event width $n$ and the same initial edge path and vertex. Given an arbitrary signed word in $B_n$, one can decide whether it can be executed *up to braid equality* from $H$ to $J$, and return a legal signed spelling if so. In particular the word problem, ambient subgroup membership, and recognition of **all abelian history groups** are decidable. On every abelian component there is a decision for arbitrary degree-four surface judgments, allowing nonhomogeneous directed attachments. The generally undecidable question from Response 60 is membership in the monoid of conjugated defects, even though membership in the underlying history group is decidable.

Write the right orthogonal fraction of the input braid as $A B^{-1}$ with $A,B$ positive and no common nonidentity right divisor. Execute $A$ positively from $H$ and $B$ positively from $J$. Accept exactly when both executions exist and reach the same temporal history. Concatenate the first path with the inverse of the second. Any positive spelling of either fraction part can be used: every positive Artin move on an executable path gives a legal replacement with the same ends. The test checks each rewrite's updated spatial position. [Positioned Artin lifting](#researcher-response-10) · [Right orthogonal splitting](#researcher-response-62)

For necessity take a legal signed path. At a valley consisting of a negative edge followed by a positive one, cancel an inverse pair or use the commuting square or the adjacent three-event hexagon at the common source. These are exactly right word-reversing moves on braid letters, including the adjusted positions of their endpoints. The finite-type braid reversing calculation yields a positive-negative fraction, and every replacement is a homotopy relative to the two temporal endpoints. Equivalently the common-successor argument of Response 10 supplies such a fraction. If its positive legs have a common right atom, use positive Artin moves on each leg to expose that atom as the final edge. At a given terminal history a positive edge with given letter has **at most one predecessor**: if the left rewrite replaces $u$ by $v$, recover the old right position from the new right position by adding $|u|-|v|$. Thus cancelling the common atom leaves two positive legs still ending at the same history. Repetition gives the right orthogonal fraction. Its uniqueness proves the test. It also proves faithfulness on fixed endpoints: two legal signed paths for the same ambient braid are homotopic to the same fraction path, since legal execution of a particular spelling from a fixed history is unique.

In the spanning tree construction of Response 77, retain the signed position word of each path from the root. Each nontree generator is then an explicit braid, namely the tree path out, its positive edge, and the inverse tree path back. For each pair of surviving generators compare the products in the two orders using the faithful Artin action on a free group. The component group is abelian exactly when every comparison succeeds. In that case abelianize its computed finite presentation and solve integer feasibility: allow the relation exponent vectors in both directions and the directed defect vectors with nonnegative coefficients. This decides the surface comparison even if abelianness is not apparent in the displayed relators. In the birth–death example of Response 77 the ambient subgroup is exactly $\langle1221\rangle\le B_3$; a braid of exponent four need not belong to it. [Finite history group and surface presentation](#researcher-response-77)

A schedule $s=(B_1,\ldots,B_d)$ partitions all the events into ordered nonempty batches, with every strict predecessor in an earlier batch. Write $I_i=B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_i$. Over this schedule use the space $H_s$ of choices $z_i\in Z_{I_{i-1},B_i}$ and paths
$$
 x\leadsto a z_1,\qquad b z_i\leadsto a z_{i+1},\qquad b z_d\leadsto y
$$
at the indicated cuts. The initial and final configurations $x,y$ are fixed. Splitting a batch substitutes the appropriate endpoint blocks at the other sites and inserts a constant path at the new cut. The raw mapping space is the homotopy colimit of the $H_s$ with maps **from coarser to finer schedules**.

Here are details of this mapping-space assertion. Resolve the directed cube $[1]^B$ by a space-enriched category with its corners as objects. From one corner to a larger corner use the permutohedron on their set of differing indices, a point for one index, with identities at equal corners. Composition is the face inclusion for an ordered split; the product identifications on faces compose by ordered refinement. Equivalently use the nerves of the face posets of the permutohedra, where the composition identifications are literal. All its comparable homs are contractible. Relative to all proper subcubes the sole new generating hom is the full-corner hom, attached along the boundary of its permutohedron. Indeed its proper faces are exactly composites through an intermediate corner, with intersections their common refinements. Induction from edges attaches each such generator by a cofibration of spaces along the free enriched arrow functor. This gives a cofibrant resolution relative to the vertices and computes the derived cube attachments. [Rigidification of directed cubes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.13679)

For a family $Z\times[1]^B$ the same relative attachment at the two outside groupoids is tensored with its endpoint bimodule. At $u,v$ this bimodule is the homotopy sum over $z\in Z$ of paths $u\leadsto az$ and $bz\leadsto v$. A bimodule map out of it classifies a natural family at those endpoints by Yoneda. Specifying the new generating hom relative to its boundary therefore has exactly the extension property for a $Z$-family of the resolved cubes with all faces given. In a composite of these attachments the relative tensor over each intermediate groupoid replaces the two endpoint paths by one intervening path, by the representable coend. Thus for a schedule the coefficient of its product of permutohedra is precisely $H_s$. The boundary of the product glues by the batch splittings above. More explicitly filter the enriched word construction by the total dimension $\sum_i(|B_i|-1)$ of those products: their interiors are free words of generating homs and their boundaries compose the specified proper faces. This also constructs the derived attachment inductively, since the boundary-to-product inclusions are cofibrations and the endpoint coefficients and relative tensors are taken in spaces. Barycentrically subdividing each product gives the homotopy-colimit formula: a simplex is a chain of face refinements carrying a point of the space at its coarsest member. This justification accounts for motions of the sites themselves, including while their two execution orders are exchanged. [Enriched composition over the intermediate groupoids](#researcher-response-78)

The complex $K$ of these products without coefficients is contractible. In the open cube of event times impose $t_e<t_f$ for $e<f$; the result is nonempty and convex. Stratify by the total preorder of the times. The strata are exactly the schedules. To verify the nerve calculation, triangulate the closed cube by ordering coordinates and barycentrically subdivide. The open convex region is the union of relative interiors of the allowed faces, with times strictly between the two endpoints and all required inequalities strict. Normalize the barycentric weights on the allowed members of each face chain, sending weights on the other members to zero. Some allowed member has positive weight everywhere in this region, and straight interpolation stays there. This retracts the region onto the order complex of the strata, which is also the subdivision of $K$ (reversing the order has the same nerve realization).

### The first homotopy groups for arbitrary dependence

For $n\ge3$ every $H_s$ is $(n-3)$-connected. The base of its endpoint path fibration is a product of $(n-2)$-connected configuration spaces, and its fibre is a product of paths in such spaces. The map from the homotopy colimit to $K$ is $(n-2)$-connected: it is the colimit in spaces of the objectwise $(n-2)$-connected maps $H_s\to *$, and connected maps of a fixed connectivity are closed under colimits of arrows (by orthogonality to truncated maps). Contractibility of $K$ gives the same $(n-3)$-connectivity for the total mapping space. The glued boundary sphere in degree $k\ge n+3$ has dimension $k-n-2$ there, and degree $n+2$ asks for connectivity. This proves reflection through $2n-1$, using the lifted graph also at the two-arrow boundary.

Now let $n\ge4$ and set $r=n-2$. The first possible group $\pi_r$ is $H_r$ by Hurewicz. It is the **abelian colimit** of the groups $H_r(H_s)$. Indeed the homotopy-colimit homology spectral sequence has constant row $H_0$, whose positive derived colimits vanish by contractibility of $K$, and vanishing rows from 1 through $r-1$. No differential can affect the stated colimit in total degree $r$. For one schedule the incidence calculation of Response 78 applies to batches: in the homotopy sequence both endpoint maps are split injective, and the first coordinate of the incidence map eliminates the first site parameter, then the next. Thus its $H_r$ is generated by
$$
 A_I=\pi_{n-1} X_I
$$
at the visited cuts, with relations transferring the images of a batch-site group between its two endpoints. These are integral pair-coordinate groups. Under a refinement the classes at a retained cut go to the identical cut classes: represent them by variation of just that path at fixed site parameters.

In the total colimit take one $A_I$ per ideal. This suffices because the schedules visiting a given cut are connected by refinements and their inverses that keep the cut: order the events before and after it independently, using adjacent swaps of incomparable consecutive events. The resulting presentation has just the relations
$$
       a_*v\text{ at } I\ =\ b_*v\text{ at } I\cup\{e\},
       \qquad v\in\pi_{n-1}Z_{I,\{e\}}.                         \tag{17}
$$
Every enabled edge extends to a full schedule. Conversely each batch relation follows along any refinement into singletons by using the endpoint substitutions on the other sites. Since the schedule groups are generated by their cuts, the refinement maps add no further relations.

For a cut $J$ take the raw substitution to the pure colours of its live wires from Response 78, concentrating the output names onto one input when proceeding backwards through $J$, and the input names onto one output when proceeding forwards through its complement. Any linear extensions of these two sets give valid assignments to all wires; incomparable steps assign disjoint ports. Corresponding raw rule paths exist by pure connectivity. The substitution maps $A_J$ identically on pair coordinates. If $I$ does not contain $J$, take a maximal $e$ of $J$ missing from $I$ (all successors in $J$ of any missing event are missing). All names of the output block of $e$ are carried together on a single wire at $I$. Indeed, looking backwards from $e$, concentration assigns them together to a single predecessor wire at every visited event. This traces one path up to $e$, consisting only of events in $J$, and the cut $I$ before $e$ intersects it in one wire. Thus the map on configurations from $I$ groups that entire block, and on $A_I$ its image lies in the image of the endpoint map $b_*$ for $J-\{e\}\to J$. For precision, substitute first a single new site for these names inside their carrier wire, keeping any other names on that wire; then insert the output block at this site. The two resulting choices of the internal configuration are connected in the ordered configuration space and induce homotopic maps. Fixed translations by the chosen rule paths have no effect on these simply connected basepoint identifications.

These cut tests jointly inject the group (17) into the product of the pure pair groups. Represent a class in their kernel by a sum over cuts and eliminate the entries in reverse order of inclusion. In the test at $J$, every other remaining cut misses some maximal event of $J$. The entry at $J$ therefore belongs to the sum of the incoming $b_*$ images. Transfer it to predecessors by (17) and continue. At the empty cut the remaining entry itself vanishes. At an old $2n$-type the proposed surface filler supplies a filler in each pure test whenever that surface is conservative there. Injectivity and the fixed-hom globe comparison return a raw filler at the specified lifted boundary and folding gives the original claim. ### Planar rules in all dimensions

For $n=2$ we can account for the whole homotopy colimit, with arbitrarily many concurrent rules. Let $M$ be the finite set of all full initial-to-final paths of the supported graph $N$, including the paths on stationary wires. Use each member of $M$ as a distinct scalar name. Substitute on each wire the composite of the names of all paths through it. At an event the input groups and the output groups partition the very same set of names. Send the event to a chosen raw connecting arrow between their composites. This gives a raw substitution into pure planar scalars and hence a functor on the fixed hom into the groupoid $Y$ of ordered configurations on $M$ in this multigrade. At a cut each name occurs once. On $X_I$ the map is block insertion with a nonempty block on **every** wire. It is injective on fundamental groups by retaining one representative per block. The same holds on any cube coefficient $Z_{I,B}$ by first inserting its input blocks into $X_I$. All these spaces and $Y$ are aspherical. Thus the pullback of the universal cover of $Y$ to each coefficient, including the cut groupoids, has contractible components.

Use these components as labels on the cubes of the ideal complex: take one cube for each component on $Z_{I,B}$, with face labels given by restriction. Call the resulting cubical complex $U$. Here the choice of which lift occurs at the other end of an edge uses the path assigned to that event. To see the compatibility for a whole cube, the substitution gives a map on $Z_{I,B}\times[1]^B$ into the groupoid $Y$, hence a local system of lifts on it. Restriction to any corner induces the same set of total components, since the cube is contractible. Its face identifications agree on intersections by restriction of the local system. This works also with homotopy coherent attaching maps since passage to component sets takes each specified homotopy to equality.

Fix a lift of the starting configuration $x$. In a schedule coefficient the initial, intervening and final paths and the cube traversals lift uniquely from that choice, up to a contractible choice of transport within a filled cube. Their endpoint over $y$ is locally constant and preserved by schedule refinement. Equivalently pull back the universal cover at each path and cube in the formula for $H_s$ and concatenate the lifted paths. With a given ending lift, this gives exactly the corresponding union of components of $H_s$: composing the traversals into $Y$ determines that lift, and path lifting recovers all intermediate lifts. In the lifted diagram the spaces at the cuts and batch parameters are disjoint unions of contractible spaces. Consequently its schedule coefficient is equivalent to the discrete set of chains of lifted cubes with matching corner labels, starting and ending at the chosen lifted vertices. Indeed for each such chain the parameter spaces and all endpoint path spaces in their respective components are contractible. These equivalences to component sets commute with refinement. The raw mapping space therefore splits over ending lifts, with the homotopy type in each part given by the order complex of directed cube chains in $U$ between the specified vertices. The interval with $d$ events traversed always has height difference $d$ in the ideal complex.

We verify nonpositive curvature of $U$. A cube is embedded since all its corners have different ideals. At a vertex over $I$ consider a set of incident edges pairwise spanning squares. Their projected directions are distinct and pairwise span squares at $I$. In the ideal complex this means that the events may be toggled independently: incoming directions remove maximal elements, outgoing ones add minimal elements of the complement, and an incoming element cannot be a predecessor of a compatible outgoing one. Their wire blocks at $I$ are disjoint. These directions span a unique cube downstairs.

Choose a base configuration at $I$ by expanding the corner of this full cube, and let $G=\pi_1 X_I$ there. At that vertex a particular lift of the $i$-th direction specifies a left coset of $H_i\subset G$, the image of the site group from clustering its wire block. Indeed the selected component of the cover of $X_I$ is universal, and its pullback to the incident site space has components the cosets of the image of its fundamental group. Use the same lift of the corner basepoint for all directions. For any subset of directions the cosets for its higher cubes are computed in just this way using their simultaneous site space: restriction to the chosen corner of a cube identifies all choices of its lift there. These descriptions apply alike to output clusters of incoming edges and input clusters of outgoing ones.

Use the complete graph configuration operad, taking the attaching configurations to fixed graph vertices by endpoint transport. Forget all but one representative in a cluster and reinsert its chosen block. This gives a based idempotent on the middle configuration space at the chosen expanded basepoint, since a singleton has a unique configuration. These idempotents commute for disjoint clusters by operad substitution. Their induced endomorphisms $p_i$ of $G$ have images $H_i$ and the image of their product is the subgroup of the simultaneous site, since all expansions split. In particular that subgroup is $\bigcap_i H_i$. [Strict configuration substitutions and erasure](#researcher-response-63)

For clarity, cosets of these subgroups have the following intersection property **in the nonabelian group**. Suppose the cosets in the proposed family meet pairwise. After finding $x$ in the first few cosets, translate by $x^{-1}$ so these are the subgroups $H_i$. The new coset $yH$ meets each $H_i$, say in $w_i$. Since $p_i(w_i)=w_i$ and $p_i(H)\subset H$ by commutation, $p_i(yH)\subset w_iH=yH$. Apply the product of the previous projections to $y$. Its value lies in all the previous subgroups and still lies in the new coset. Induction gives a common element. The intersection is a single coset of $\bigcap_i H_i$. The edge lifts therefore belong to precisely one cube of $U$. For pairs the same common-coset calculation rules out multiple corners with the same two edge germs. This proves the links are simplicial and flag; the cubical link condition gives a CAT(0) universal cover in each component. This reasoning allows many different incident lifts of an individual direction. [Cubical link condition](https://www.imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr/~frederic.haglund/special%28corrected%29.pdf)

Lift the cube chains once more to this ordinary universal cover, fixing their first vertex. The label of the ending lift is again unchanged by refinement, and all chains are recovered by projecting from the respective lifts. Each directed edge raises the integer height $|I|$ by one. A directed edge path, between any fixed two such lifted vertices, has length their height difference and is a combinatorial geodesic, because a single edge changes height by at most one. Conversely, once a directed path exists, every edge geodesic between these vertices is directed by the same length calculation. The cubical interval between two vertices in a CAT(0) cube complex is the ideal complex of their finite poset of separating hyperplanes: its vertices are the intermediate ideals and its geodesics are their linear extensions. This interval description uses only the finitely many separating hyperplanes, including when the ambient complex has infinite valence. A cube traversed by a directed chain lies entirely in the interval, as all its vertices can occur in serial refinements. Conversely every positively traversed cube of the interval supplies the corresponding batch. Thus at these two lifts the cube-chain poset consists of **all** schedules of that hyperplane poset. Its nerve is contractible by the event-time argument above. [Ardila–Owen–Sullivant, interval posets and edge geodesics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.2428)

It follows that every planar named raw arrow mapping space here is homotopy discrete. For degree at least five even an arbitrary old parallel boundary lifts on both faces starting with the same occurrence names: its common raw arrow face fixes the supported graph, and raw state propagation fixes its literal common boundary. Its sphere in that mapping space has positive dimension and is null. Folding supplies a filler. Raw 4-cells have reverses since the hom above dimension three is groupoidal. Response 5 proves conservativity in lower degrees for all ten surfaces, and Response 31 now gives their conservativity through $h+1$ after arbitrary higher declarations first attached in degree $h\ge4$. These consequences allow repeated uses of the same original rule and independent events whose middle braids prevent a simultaneous execution in a specified path class. ### A nonabelian obstruction at rank three

Take two disjoint named rules, each consuming two distinct scalar colours and producing two fresh ones. Use all four initial wires once and all four terminal wires once, with no stationary wires outside the two rules. The schedule complex for the raw mapping space is an interval. It gives the homotopy pushout of the two serial spaces over the simultaneous space. All three are connected. By the incidence calculation of Response 78 the two serial fundamental groups are free abelian of rank $3\binom42-2\binom32=12$, and the simultaneous one has rank $2\binom42-\binom22=11$. Its maps use precisely the two exterior cuts in the serial presentations.

Both maps split injectively with cyclic cokernel. For injectivity, an exterior relation in a serial presentation has cancelling images of its two site parameters in the middle $\pi_2 X$. Their common image lies in the image of the simultaneous site group by the same disjoint idempotents, now applied to $\pi_2$. This gives the relation already in the simultaneous group. The cokernel is the middle pair group modulo the two expanded-site images. They contain the two internal pair generators, one from each stationary block. On the four cross pairs they impose the two row sums and the two column sums of a $2\times2$ array, after orienting pairs from the first block to the second. The quotient is infinite cyclic, with the coordinates evaluated by alternating signs. Van Kampen now gives the indicated direct product of the common central lattice with the free group on the two remaining letters. In particular the commutator of lifts of the two cyclic generators is nontrivial. Represent it and the constant loop at the same raw arrow by parallel old 5-cells using the fixed-hom globe comparison; there is no raw 6-filler. A substitution into a pure rank-three scalar presentation lands in a path space of a configuration groupoid at these endpoints. The fundamental group of any component of that path space is abelian, even after identifying colours. Hence the commutator always maps to zero. This is why the abelian colimit proof in degree $2n$ requires $n\ge4$. It leaves the unrestricted classification and this rank-three surface test open. ∎

**Validation.** The checker compared path-weight exact covers with cuts and concurrent batches on all 64 forward-edge sets on four events, finding 1,444 matching frontiers. At the independent square the edge relations have rank 11 in 24 pair generators and the cut images have rank 13. A branching three-event diagram gave ranks 10 and 6 in 16 generators. The composites with the relations vanished for both antipodal signs. The middle-cut alternating characters annihilated both incident images and their two free letters had nontrivial commutator in a matrix quotient. On actual planar braids, the Artin action verified 100 double cablings and the common-coset test on 64 six-strand triples, of which 20 admitted a lift. Rice's raw and SUA checkers accepted the two-rule exchange at its exact rank-three scalar boundary and rejected it with the ports exchanged. Both also checked a raw degree-five round trip at three independent planar two-input, two-output rules. Run `python3 tools/semistrict_surface_concurrent_rules.py --catt-strict /path/to/catt-strict` with SymPy available. The arbitrary-poset and homotopy-group conclusions use the proofs above. Together with the pure-permutation-preserving case of Response 68 this gives the asserted exhaustive decision.

There is a stronger obstruction when other defects are present. At this same test width suppose every available rule satisfies $a\ge c d$. Equality of the total cost with $c$ times the distance again forces every effective step to be distance-optimal and the whole factorization to be shortest, after splitting each defect into transpositions. The first defect must therefore be a product of a subset of the specified $c$ disjoint pairs. Indeed every initial segment of a shortest factorization is obtained by successively splitting the unspent cycles of $Q$; in a matching each split takes just one of its pairs. For a subset of size $s$ the inversion length is $s(2c-s)$. Each transposition alone has length $2c-1$ and each pair of interleaved transpositions reduces their combined length by two, as seen on their four endpoints. For $0<s<c$ this exceeds the available $cs$. The only possible first effective step spends the entire $c^2$ and outputs $Q$. At the empty source the outer positive contexts have zero length, so this requires a literal empty-source rule with that target permutation and count at some consecutive placement. In its absence the same boundary certifies failure. This test also explains why checking all single signed steps between positive endpoints can miss a multi-step comparison: for the block swap even granting *all* such transposition steps leaves no possible positive seam.

Along a raw comparison every intermediate count is at most $K+C$. An effective step has permutation multiplier $u q p^{-1}u^{-1}$, where the rule on $p,q$ is placed in a window of width at most $w$ and the positive outer context permutation $u$ has a word of length at most $K+C$. Thus its support lies inside the window enlarged by at most $K+C$ positions at either end. There are at most $C$ costly steps. Each connected component of the union of their support intervals has length at most $C(w+2(K+C))$. The total product in any one component is obtained using just its steps. Every displayed cycle lies in a single component, and no component can meet two displayed cycles. The cost spent in a component with one terminal cycle therefore belongs to its individual signed cost set. ## Researcher Response 90

**Degree six on rank-three scalar networks.** For every finite positive named network of Response 82 there is a presentation of the *full fundamental group* of its raw arrow space by the cuts and the order relation between cuts. If the event order is an ordinal sum of disjoint unions of chains, this group is a right-angled Artin group. Consequently every old 6-type in such a component that is inhabited under published insertion, or under binary $\{A,U\}$, has a raw inhabitant. Each chain can have arbitrary positive input and output arities, bypass wires, and arbitrary length. The test concerns occurrence networks, so it applies also to a boundary lifted from repeated original colours as in Response 86. [Named occurrence networks](#researcher-response-82) · [Directed reflection criterion](#researcher-response-86)

### A group presentation for arbitrary event dependence

For a cut $I$ let $V_I$ be the free integral lattice on its live wires, and put $A_I=\bigwedge^2 V_I$. For an enabled event $e$ let $V_{I,e}$ have one basis element for the site and one per stationary wire. Its maps $a,b$ into $V_I,V_{I+e}$ fix the stationary basis and send the site to the sum of its input, respectively output, wires. Then $G$ has one copy of each group $A_I$, with precisely the following additional relations:
$$
 [A_I,A_J]=1\quad(I\subseteq J),\qquad
 (\bigwedge^2 a)v=(\bigwedge^2 b)v
 \quad(v\in\bigwedge^2 V_{I,e}).
$$
Here the two terms of the second relation belong to the successive cut groups. Exchanging the order of an oriented pair on the configuration sphere in three-space has degree $-1$. Cabling a port replaces its oriented pair with another carrier by the sum of all the expanded oriented pairs. These two facts give the exterior-square formula for the actual maps on $\pi_2$.

We first justify the basepoints needed for this *group* presentation. Use little 3-disks for the configuration coefficients of the schedule diagram $H_s$ in Response 82. Choose disjoint event balls. Inside each ball place its two prescribed port configurations. They may be moved into two disjoint smaller balls first. Indeed each ordered space of port configurations is path connected, and homotoping the two attaching maps along those paths induces an equivalence of the derived free arrow attachments relative to the pure part. Choose initial and final disks freely as well, transporting back along configuration paths at the ends. For each wire choose a path of little disks from its output port or initial disk to its input port or final disk. Require its path to miss every nonincident event ball, and the paths of coexisting wires to have disjoint disks at *all* parameter pairs. To construct them, take mutually disjoint narrow exits from the finite port configurations inside the event balls, shrinking the disks along the exits, and join their ends by disjoint polygonal arcs in the complement of the ball interiors. Successive arcs can be perturbed off the finitely many previous arcs in three-space relative to their distinct ends. Use sufficiently thin tubes and reverse the shrinking at the terminal ports. The event site itself can now coexist with any stationary disk of that batch.

For each schedule $s$ take a product $T_s$ of simplices. Its factor at a wire specifies nondecreasing sample times in $[0,1]$ for the batches at which that wire is stationary, in chronological order. Take time zero at birth and one at consumption, including the outside ends. Map $T_s\to H_s$ by using the chosen event sites and the sampled stationary disks at each batch. On the connecting pure paths advance each live wire linearly between its two sample times on its own path. When a batch splits, duplicate a stationary wire's sample at both parts. A wire first made stationary by this split has time zero after its producing part, or time one before its consuming part. No wire connects two events in the same batch. The inserted middle path is therefore constant at exactly the expanded site configuration. On further splits each sample is still either a copy of the original sample or the same prescribed endpoint. This constructs a natural map of diagrams from nonempty contractible $T_s$, for every event order.

Objectwise form the homotopy pushout $H_s\cup^h_{T_s}*$ using mapping cylinders. It is equivalent to $H_s$ and gives a based diagram. The schedule nerve is contractible by Response 82. Collapsing its basepoint section in the homotopy colimit is thus a weak equivalence (use the simplicial replacement with cofibrant basepoints). For connected based spaces, the fundamental group of this pointed homotopy colimit is the colimit of the fundamental groups: based maps to every $K(\pi,1)$ form homotopically discrete spaces with components the group homomorphisms, so their homotopy limit computes precisely the compatible families. For an individual schedule the endpoint fibration gives an abelian fundamental group generated by the pair groups at its cuts, modulo the batch incidence relations. Indeed the base is simply connected, and its second homotopy group maps into the first homotopy group of the path fibre by the two endpoint expansions with opposite signs. This description is independent of paths to basepoints in that schedule since its group is abelian. Refinement retains the names of pair classes at each retained cut. The schedules through any one cut are connected by adjacent exchanges on its two sides, and every pair of comparable cuts occurs in a serial schedule. Finally each batch incidence follows by transferring the same class along a singleton refinement, expanding the sites of the other batch members at the appropriate ends. These facts give exactly the displayed group presentation. [Schedule spaces and cubical realization](#researcher-response-82)

### Integral wire bases along a chain

Along a chain of $m$ events write $V_k$ for the lattice after $k$ events. At each step the site lattice maps injectively to each end, as the sublattice whose coordinates on the incident ports are equal. Transfer across the step is the isomorphism of these sublattices. We claim there are integral bases at all cuts and sites in which both maps simply retain named basis vectors, each name occurring on a single interval.

At cut $k$ filter $V_k$ by the sublattices of vectors extending by transfer back to cut $i$, for $i=0,\ldots,k$. Filter it also by the vectors extending forward to cut $j$, for $j=m,\ldots,k$. Both are increasing flags ending in $V_k$; start both with zero. Each nonzero stage is a partition sublattice. A vector extends precisely when it is constant on the wires belonging to each connected component of the slab between the two cuts. Transfer equates all entries incident to each event there. Conversely assign the constant value to every wire in that component. Every component reaches the specified cut, by positivity on both sides of every event. This proves the description including stationary wires.

Write $F_i,L_j$ for the two flags in increasing order and $H_{ij}=F_i\cap L_j$. Each nonzero intersection is again block-constant, for the equivalence relation generated by the two partitions. In $H_{ij}$ the sum $H_{i-1,j}+H_{i,j-1}$ has free cokernel. In coordinates indexed by the blocks of $H_{ij}$, form the bipartite multigraph with a vertex for each block of each of the two coarser partitions and one edge per coordinate. The two sublattices together are the image of the vertex-to-edge coboundary map, changing sign on one side. On a spanning forest arbitrary edge values can be prescribed by successive vertex potentials. A potential with zero difference on that forest has zero difference everywhere. Thus the unit vectors on the other edges give a free complement. If one sublattice is zero use one representative coordinate per block of the other sublattice, and if both vanish use the whole coordinate basis.

Choose bases of these complements in increasing row and column order. They give a simultaneous integral basis for the flags since the intersection of the two previously spanned sublattices is $H_{i-1,j-1}$. This construction extends any prescribed simultaneous basis inside a whole row $F_i$: retain its vectors there, and start adjoining complements at the following row. At cut zero choose a simultaneous basis. At a step retain the basis vectors spanning the site image on the old side, a stage of the forward flag. Transfer them across. They give precisely a simultaneous basis on the row of the new backward flag consisting of vectors extending across that step. On that row, extension to any earlier cut is the old backward condition, and extension to any later cut is the old forward condition under transfer. Intersections have the same description. Extend from this row by the complement construction, giving fresh names to the added vectors. Induction proves the claim over $\mathbb Z$.

### Computing the group and reflecting a filler

In a disjoint union of chains each cut is a tuple of chain indices. Assign stationary external wires their own constant lattices. There are no wires between event chains, as such a wire would impose dependence. The preceding bases give a basis of $V_I$ by direct sum. Take a fixed total ordering of all basis names. The basis of $A_I$ consists of the ordered wedges of two distinct names present at $I$. The support of each resulting pair is a box of cuts: its coordinate on a chain runs in the intersection of the relevant intervals, and unrestricted coordinates run over the entire chain. Ignore empty boxes. Singleton incidences identify the same wedge on adjacent cuts of the box, and only such wedges. Each box is connected by those edges. The presentation therefore has one generator per box **with its pair name retained**, even if several boxes coincide. Two generators commute exactly as prescribed by an edge of the following graph: their boxes contain cuts $I,J$ with $I\subseteq J$ or $J\subseteq I$. Indeed an incidence only identifies basis generators, and the within-schedule relations are precisely the commutations already in the presentation. This is the defining presentation of a right-angled Artin group. The basis at either outside cut is a subset of universal vertices, because that cut is comparable with every cut.

At a seam between two ordinal stages the cut groups of one stage commute with every cut group of the other. The seam lattice is the same lattice on the two sides. Hence the full presentation takes the direct product of the stage groups and identifies the two copies of that lattice. In each stage write the group as a central free lattice times the Artin group on the remaining vertices, putting all universal vertices in the central lattice. Each outside cut is a direct summand there. Identifying the seam in the two central lattices gives a free lattice into which each original central lattice still includes as a direct summand: split the seam off the opposite side to see the retraction and free complement. The two remaining Artin groups form a direct product, again a right-angled Artin group by the graph join. The new outside cuts remain direct summands of the central lattice. This proves the assertion by induction, including stages whose bases at a shared seam differ.

Every right-angled Artin group is residually torsion-free nilpotent. Thus Response 86 detects every nontrivial difference loop of two parallel old 5-cells on these networks. A trivial difference loop gives a raw 6-cell at that boundary by the fixed-hom globe comparison, and the supported lift folds back to the original old type. This proves the claimed reflection. [Wade, Theorem 4.12](https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/44295) · [Directed comparison at old faces](#researcher-response-86)

For example take two independent chains of two successive two-input, two-output uses each, with both outputs consumed at the next use on that chain. Each wire basis consists of a constant vector throughout and one additional vector at each individual cut. The group has 22 generators and nine unordered pairs without a commutation relation. In particular the three pair names supported only at $(0,2),(1,1),(2,0)$ freely generate a retract: send every other generator to the identity. The nested commutator of those three classes is an unfilled old 6-boundary even under insertion. Mapping the three letters to the successive elementary generators of $\mathrm{UT}_4(\mathbb Z)$ detects it in the top right entry.

There is a concrete limit to the interval-basis proof. Take three independent events $a_{12},a_{23},a_{13}$, each with one external input and two outputs, one going to each indicated $b_i,b_j$. Each $b_i$ consumes its two inputs and has one final wire. In the lattice on the three final wires, transfer back across $b_i,b_j,a_{ij}$ is possible precisely on the plane $x_i=x_j$. The three distinct planes have a common line. Three distinct coordinate planes of an integral basis in rank three have zero common intersection. Hence no single wire basis at this cut can make all those transfers coordinate inclusions. The group presentation above still applies to this network. Residual torsion-free nilpotence for arbitrary dependence, and the unrestricted classifications in Q1 and Q2, remain open here. ∎

On the two-chain grid it recovered the 22 generators and nine missing commutations, then tested the unitriangular representation directly on all 12 original cut incidences and every comparable pair of cut groups. Its nested commutator has top right entry one. For two independent squares synchronized by a four-input, four-output event, the original pair maps give abelian rank 26, agreeing with $\mathbb Z^{22}\times F_2\times F_2$ from the seam calculation. ### Sorting a schedule without changing its mapping space

Suppose the enlarged graph has a linear extension $t_1,\ldots,t_d$. We show that inclusion of this single serial schedule in $H$ is a weak equivalence. Delete $t$ from the schedule poset of the remainder, discarding an empty batch. This gives a functor $D$ to schedules on the other events and a section $i$ putting $t$ alone first. The coefficient spaces throughout still include the entire prefix and the paths at its two ends.

For a schedule $a$ downstairs, the fibre of $D$ consists of the gaps where $t$ can run alone and the batches it can join. In chronological order these form a subdivided closed interval, beginning at the first gap and stopping just before the first batch containing a successor, or at the last gap if there is none. The arrows go from a joined placement to its two adjacent gaps. This fibre computes the pointwise homotopy left Kan extension over $a$. Indeed for $s$ with $D(s)$ refined by $a$, the lifts of $a$ refining $s$ form a point when $t$ was separate, and a subdivided interval when its old batch was split: the allowed placements are exactly the gaps and joins inside that batch, including both outside gaps. Their nerves are contractible. The overcategory criterion for finality now applies to the inclusion of the fibre in $(D\downarrow a)$. [Quillen's Theorem A in the cofinality criterion](https://kerodon.net/tag/02H0)

For a join with batch $B$ the map from the joined coefficient to the **following** gap, where $B$ runs and then $t$, is a weak equivalence. In the refined schedule the two sites together with their connecting pure path have parameter space $Z_B\times^h_{X_{\rm mid}} Z_t$ at these cuts. If $t$ has one input, $Z_t\to X_{\rm mid}$ is an equivalence and the joined site projects equivalently to $Z_B$ by expanding that unary input. If $t$ has several inputs, every event of $B$ has one output. Indeed these events are incomparable with $t$ and an event with several outputs would have been required to precede $t$ in the chosen extension. Now $Z_B\to X_{\rm mid}$ is an equivalence, and the joined site projects equivalently to $Z_t$ by expanding those outputs. Unary little-disks operations are homotopic to the unit. The joined site maps to the homotopy pullback by the constant middle path, with the same two outside endpoint maps. Fitting the remaining paths is a homotopy pullback, so it preserves this equivalence.

Successively taking the homotopy pushouts along the placement interval shows that inclusion of its first gap is an equivalence. It is the natural map from the section $i$ to the left Kan extension, hence an equivalence after colimit over $a$. Fixing $t$ first therefore preserves the full homotopy colimit. ### What pure substitutions miss

Suppose the enlarged graph is cyclic. It has two added requirements $f_1\to m_1$, $f_2\to m_2$ with $m_1\le f_2$ and $m_2\le f_1$ in the original order. To see this minimize the number of added edges in a cycle. One is impossible by incomparability. If there are three or more, write consecutive segments $f_1\to m_1\le f_2\to m_2\le f_3$. If $m_1\le f_3$, shorten the cycle. If $f_3\le m_1$ there would be a cycle with just one added edge. In the remaining case $f_3\to m_1$ is itself a requirement and closes a cycle with two. For each of the resulting pairs let $W_i$ be the cuts with $f_i$ executed and $m_i$ unexecuted. No cut in $W_1$ is comparable with one in $W_2$.

For $f=f_i$, put a signed flow $u$ equal to $+1,-1$ on two of its outputs and zero on all its other ports. Propagate each subsequent incoming sum onto a single output, with zero elsewhere. For $m=m_i$ use a flow $v$ defined backwards from two inputs of opposite sign. Both conserve the sum at every event. At a cut define an integer character on the first pair group by assigning the oriented pair of distinct wires $(a,b)$ the value
$$
              u(a)v(b)+(-1)^n u(b)v(a).
$$
This has the correct sign under reversal. On expansion of a site, summation over the port block is exactly conservation of the two flows; the characters respect all incidence relations. The character is zero off $W_i$. It takes value one up to sign at the cut consisting of the strict predecessors of $f,m$ together with $f$: both selected outputs of $f$ and both selected inputs of $m$ are live. The two flows have disjoint support since $f$ and $m$ are incomparable.

For $r=1$, send each cut group of Response 90 to powers of $x$ or $y$ in $F(x,y)$ using its respective character, and to the identity away from the two supports. Comparability never imposes a commutation between these two letters. The incidences agree and the unit values lift each letter, giving a retraction. The commutator of the lifts is nontrivial and its old 6-type has no published-insertion filler either, by the class-two quotient test of Response 86. It vanishes after all pure substitutions.

For $r\ge2$ the two characters give integral classes $c_i\in H^r(H;\mathbb Z)$ by (17), connectivity, Hurewicz and universal coefficients. Let $A_i$ be the sub-homotopy-colimit over schedules in which $m_i$ precedes or is tied with $f_i$. That subposet has contractible nerve: in the convex event-time region of Response 82 impose the additional closed linear inequality $t_{m_i}\le t_{f_i}$. The same barycentric retraction onto its allowed strata applies and the region is nonempty. All its coefficient spaces are $(r-1)$-connected, and its degree-$r$ homology is generated by their degree-$r$ classes. Indeed the homotopy-colimit homology sequence has constant degree-zero row on this contractible base and zero intervening rows. Each visited cut lies outside $W_i$, so $c_i|_{A_i}=0$. Use a cellular simplicial replacement, where the subdiagrams give subcomplexes. The two subcomplexes cover $H$: in any refinement chain the finest schedule can have $f_i$ strictly before $m_i$ for at most one $i$, and a strict order in a coarser schedule persists on refinement.

Represent each $c_i$ by a map to $K(\mathbb Z,r)$ constant on $A_i$, using relative cohomology and the cofibration of subcomplexes. Their product therefore gives a map from $H$ into the wedge of the two Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces. For each character take the cut sphere of a unit pair, whiskered along a serial schedule through its cut. Its image is a generator in the corresponding summand and lies wholly there, since the schedule belongs to the other $A_j$. Transport the two spheres to a common basepoint; the target wedge is simply connected. Their mixed Whitehead product is nonzero. Otherwise the wedge of their images would extend over $S^r\times S^r$, where the two fundamental cohomology classes pull back to the two coordinate generators. Their cup product vanishes on the target wedge and is nonzero on the product of spheres. This contradiction uses the attaching map of the product's top cell. [Whitehead products, Hatcher §4.2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch4.pdf)

In contrast every pure target arrow space at the substituted ends is a path space in a configuration groupoid. Its chosen component is homotopy equivalent to the identity component of a loop space by translation, also for repeated colours. Multiplication extends any two based spheres there across their product, killing their Whitehead product; in degree one the fundamental group is abelian. The fixed-hom globe test realizes the detected class against the constant class at the same raw base arrow, by parallel old faces. This gives degree $n+2+(2r-1)=3n-3$ and proves the stated sharp limit of pure detection. The argument for $r\ge2$ leaves surface inhabitation of these particular Whitehead boundaries open, as well as the unrestricted Q1 and Q2 classifications. ∎

**Validation.** Exhaustive linear extensions on four events, testing all 64 forward edge sets and all input/output multiplicity flags, gave 14,062 sortable cases and 2,322 obstructed cases. The two-requirement certificate matched every outcome. All 3,128 tested overcategory fibres were points or intervals. Both orientation signs satisfied the actual site relations on the two-event square and on an example with four distinct actors in the certificate. For three independent two-input, two-output events and for a branching network, the schedule bar differential and the cubical differential independently squared to zero over the integers, with matching homology concentrated in degree zero over $\mathbb F_2,\mathbb F_3,\mathbb F_5$ at both signs. The six-event cubical calculation gave rank 15 and all 18 cuts expanded to the middle wires. Rice’s checker accepted the full six-event computation with the terminal pairs obtained by a scalar braid. At the same old 6-type it accepted the raw unitor, accepted the converted identity under SUA and rejected that identity in raw CaTT. Run `python3 tools/semistrict_surface_serial_detection.py --catt-strict /path/to/catt-strict` and `python3 tools/semistrict_surface_schedule_homology.py` with SymPy installed. [Order, fibre, flow and typing checks](../../../tools/semistrict_surface_serial_detection.py) · [Independent schedule and cube complexes](../../../tools/semistrict_surface_schedule_homology.py)

At the native $k$-atom its tensor differential has two facets omitting each spatial axis $j$, numbered $0,\ldots,k-1$. The omitted strand is stationary *after* the active block at the bit-zero facet, precisely the facet scored on the first $k-1$ temporal events. At the bit-one facet it is before the block. The initial order is reverse spatial order. To put the omitted strand last costs exactly $j$ crossings before the retained facet. No other crossing can be in that prefix: all pairs exchange just once in the characteristic reversal, and the retained $(k-1)$-facet executes all pairs of its own strands. where $c_{S,L}$ counts exactly its native $k$-steps on $S$ at projected prefix length $L$. Polynomial division over the integers determines these numbers uniquely. At the bottom there are only finitely many offsets and cube ranks for the given temporal input. Test each reassembled candidate against the entire source.
