## Researcher Response 132

**At a specified old type, failure has an exact computability classification.** Fix a kernel, one of its surfaces, and a degree $k\ge3$. If the universal degree-$k$ assertion in Q1 holds, the set of failures is empty. Otherwise, on inputs consisting of a finite context and an old $k$-type, failure is complete among differences of two computably enumerable sets, under computable many-one reductions. Hardness already holds with one fixed lower skeleton and one fixed query, varying only top declarations. For each Gray surface containing $I$, the nonempty case holds in every such degree. There one may instead **fix the entire finite context** for that degree and vary only the query. In fact the same family realizes any prescribed nested pair of computably enumerable sets as its raw and surface inhabitation predicates.

### Putting a second condition on one old type

Let $u,v$ be parallel old $(k-1)$-terms in $D$, put $m=k-2$ and let $b$ be their common $m$-target. Choose any finite directed substring presentation with nonempty sides. Extend $D$ by an $m$-generator $h$ of exactly the type of $b$, two $(m+1)$-generators $o:b\to h$ and $c:h\to b$, and a loop $h\to h$ for every letter. Attach its substring rules as $k$-generators between word readings at $h$. Use top composition at cut $m$ for the letters. For nonempty words $W,V$ set
$$
 D(t,W)=t *_m ((o *_m W) *_m c).
$$
In **each theory separately**, raw or surface, the old type $D(u,W)\to D(v,V)$ has a filler exactly when $u\to v$ has a filler in the original context in that theory **and** $W\longrightarrow^* V$ in the substring presentation.

For sufficiency, carry the given filler past the stationary suffix, then carry the word derivation inside the suffix at $v$. Each substring move uses the fixed prefix and suffix of that move and the raw structural rebracketings of a temporal string. All cuts in this construction are temporal compositions or whiskerings with their literal faces.

For the first necessary condition take a raw substitution fixing the old context. Send $h$ to $b$ and the ports and letters to identities on $b$. Each new rule then has a raw interpretation on the disc for $b$, comparing two top composites of identity cells in the given direction. Its disc head has full support and equal strict faces in either kernel. Under this substitution the two query faces become $u$ and $v$ followed by bracketed identity strings. The expansion at $u$ and contraction at $v$ are raw disc comparisons with the actual parallel faces. Composing them with the substituted filler recovers the original type, also when the middle filler uses conversion.

For the second necessary condition use the ordinary strict projection, which respects all the surfaces in the question. Send the original generators to the point and its iterated identities. Keep $h$ as one generating $m$-scalar. Write the number of occurrences of $h$ in an $m$-cell as its width. The two ports now have profiles $0\to1$ and $1\to0$, and each letter has profile $1\to1$. Only the word rules remain as nonidentity $k$-generators. The projected query has source reading $oWc$ and target reading $oVc$.

Here is why strict interchange cannot change the word recognized between the two ports. For an $(m+1)$-paste define its load to be its input width plus the total number of openings in it. This quantity is unchanged by strict equations. At a cut below $m$ loads add. At cut $m$, each factor's load is at most the load of the whole paste: the intermediate width equals the input width plus prior openings minus prior closings. A load-zero paste is an identity of width zero, as follows by induction or by executing its generating steps from width zero. At load at most one, read a paste by concatenating at cut $m$, retaining the sole positive-load factor at lower cuts, and reading an identity as the empty string. This reading is invariant under strict equations. For interchange between a lower and the temporal cut, take the expression in which the two temporal composites are the two lower-cut factors. One entire composite has load zero, so the other supplies the same ordered reading on both sides. Interchange between two lower cuts retains at most one contributing factor. Associativity, units and composites of identities preserve the reading directly.

Serialize any projected $k$-paste into single generating steps in composition contexts, by expanding compositions into whiskered steps followed in time. Every intermediate $(m+1)$-face still starts at width zero and has exactly one opening, since none of the word rules changes the opening count. Consequently every such face and every subexpression used to read it has load at most one. At a temporal cut the context puts fixed words before and after the rewritten substring. At a lower cut, the rule acts at width one, so the other factor contributes nothing. Each step therefore changes just its indicated substring in the reading. The rules use letters only and the end delimiters $o,c$ persist. This gives an actual derivation from $W$ to $V$, including when $m>1$ and lower-dimensional interchange is strict. This proves the equivalence.

### Realizing both predicates

On arbitrary finite inputs failure is the difference of the set with a surface derivation and the set with a raw derivation. Both can be enumerated by finite proof trees, including equational proofs for a binary surface. For the lower bound suppose a failure in degree $k$ exists. By [Response 129](#researcher-response-129) there is a computable family with a fixed old query that always has a surface filler and has a raw filler exactly upon acceptance of a machine input $y$. Apply the construction above, using an independent universal recognizer on input $x$ for the word problem. Use a fixed initial letter $J$, a fixed cleaned accepting letter $F$, and one additional rule $J\to Lq_0xR$. On a delimited initial configuration the positive rules simulate the machine and produce $F$ exactly upon acceptance, as in [Response 123](#researcher-response-123). Use private letters for this second computation. At the new fixed type with words $J,F$, the surface predicate is now acceptance of $x$ and the raw predicate is acceptance of both $x$ and $y$. For any computably enumerable sets $A,B$, supply recognizers for $z\in A$ and $z\in B$ as these two inputs. This reduces $A\setminus B$ to failure. All varying declarations have degree $k$.

For the fixed-context Gray version use the **fixed-presentation** construction of [Response 123](#researcher-response-123) for $y$. Its query varies with $y$, but its common $m$-target is always the same raw term $b_0*_{m-1}h_0$, since all the letters on its final suffix loop at the same tape generator $h_0$. The second tape can therefore be attached once, at this one literal interface. Use the fixed universal rules and take $W=Lq_0xR$, $V=F$ in the query. This time the entire context is independent of $x,y$. Taking $B\subseteq A$ gives raw predicate $B$ and surface predicate $A$ simultaneously for all four interchange surfaces. In particular there is neither an enumeration of all failures nor an enumeration of all nonfailures at old types of this fixed context: taking $B$ empty realizes a nondecidable enumerable failure set, and taking $A$ universal realizes its complement. This answers the pointwise computability question; deciding which side of the opening dichotomy applies to the remaining ordinary surfaces and to Gray $\{A,U\}$ still requires Q1.

**Validation.** The [independent tape checker](../../../tools/semistrict_surface_independent_tape.py) constructs the port substitution on every declaration and checks the resulting literal boundary after a two-letter rule and an independent old move. Generate with `--agda-dir DIR` and check the emitted ordinary and Gray modules with `agda --safe -i src -i DIR`. They check both carrying the two moves and recovering the old filler in degrees three, four and five. The checker also enumerates all 137 pairs of temporal paths of length at most four per factor and total load at most one over two letters and both ports, verifying the reading under every interleaving. The proof above gives the unbounded load-one invariant.

\begin{array}{ll}
\exists d:f'\to f, & a d\le 1_f\quad\text{and}\quad 1_{f'}\le d a,\\
\text{or}\quad\exists e:g'\to g, &1_g\le b e\quad\text{and}\quad e b\le 1_{g'} .
\end{array}                                                     \tag{1}
$$
Separation allows any edge path between the inner object poles and repeated uses of one generator. The finite conjunction is recursively enumerable by searching for the directed certificates.

### Following two cuts through a return

Use the ordered-list presentation and its exact-boundary lifting theorem in [Response 2](#researcher-response-2). In a fixed spatial word every event has a position: all 2-generators preserve the number and positions of the edges. A local 3-move replaces a consecutive same-position sublist by its declared output. A native exchange moves an event at a smaller spatial position earlier. Conversely these contextual moves lift at the specified raw faces, with rebracketings in the temporal arities. In checking a proposed return retain just the two positions in the square, calling them left and right. Forget the others. A move at another site or an exchange involving an omitted event gives equality of the projected lists. Moves at the two retained sites remain typed because their edge labels change only there. The result runs from $a b$ to $b a$.

In the left projection mark a prefix, initially the whole letter $a$. In the right projection mark a suffix, initially the whole letter $b$. For a left replacement starting after $i$ letters with input length $l$ and output length $q$, update the prefix length $c$ by
$$
 c' = \begin{cases}
 c & c\le i,\\
 i+q & i<c\le i+l,\\
 c-l+q & i+l<c .
 \end{cases}
$$
Update a right suffix by the same rule read from the other end. A native swap leaves both projected cuts unchanged. At every stage all marked left letters precede all marked right letters in the mixed list. Indeed, a replacement wholly on the unmarked side does not advance the marked cut; a replacement strictly inside the prefix has an old marked letter at or after its far end, except for the consumed last letter, in which case the replacement itself is at that position. If the replacement straddles the cut, its contiguous block includes a marked letter and contains no event at the other site. Its entire output can therefore be marked. A birth exactly at the cut is assigned to the unmarked side. The suffix proof reads in reverse temporal order. A native swap only improves the required order. At the final list $b a$ at least one of the two marked parts must consequently be empty.

Suppose the left cut vanishes. Replay just the left rewrites with a movable separator, starting at $a\mid 1_{f'}$. Execute each replacement wholly on its side when possible, putting a birth at the cut on the right. If the input straddles the cut, first transfer the missing letters across the separator from right to left, then replace the input on the left. The prefix is exactly the prefix given by the update formula, including a rewrite whose last input is just at the cut. The final state is $1_f\mid a$. Concatenating the transferred letters in chronological order gives a composable path $d:f'\to f$; its current end is the current edge label at the cut. The left-side rewrites give $a d\le 1_f$: at each stage append the as yet untransferred tail of $d$ to the left word. Transfers then leave this combined word unchanged. The right-side rewrites give $1_{f'}\le d a$ by prefixing the already transferred portion of $d$ to the current right word. This proves the first alternative with the **same** partner for both inequalities. If the right cut vanishes, reverse the temporal order of all the right words (retaining the directions of the rewrites) and perform that argument. Reversing the resulting partner and inequalities gives exactly the second alternative. This establishes necessity even when both sites repeatedly create and consume events.

Conversely, given the first alternative, start at $a b$, insert $d a$ after $b$ using the unit, and move $b$ across the letters of $d$ by native exchanges $b d_i\to d_i b$. Consume $a d$ before $b$ using the counit. This ends at $b a$. Given the second, insert $b e$ before $a$, exchange $e_i a\to a e_i$ successively from the end of $e$, and consume $e b$ after $a$. The other site is stationary while using each local unit or counit, so its current edge label is the required whisker. The same construction works across any stationary gap. Together with the elementary-return criterion of Response 2 this proves the claim.

### Exact spectra and a recognition problem

At one object every ordered pair of generators is spatially separated. Thus (1) passes throughout precisely if **every generator has a left adjoint, or every generator has a right adjoint** in the indicated local preorder. This follows by choosing a failing generator on each side if neither universal condition holds. With at least one 2-generator one may repeat it at arbitrarily many spatial positions. In a 3-computad the repeated cube of [Response 29](#researcher-response-29) gives failure in every degree $k\ge4$. The proof of that obstruction permits all the local 3-declarations considered here. Degrees below three reflect, giving the two full spectra asserted above. More generally in a multi-object 3-computad a separated triple forces failure in degree four, so (1) decides mathematically whether the first failure is three or four whenever a triple exists.

In particular take one object, one generating edge, and one generating 2-endomorphism on that edge for each letter of a nonempty alphabet. For each relator of a finite monoid presentation give both directed 3-rules. The local preorder then records precisely equality in the presented monoid. Either adjunction condition for a letter says that it is a two-sided unit. The first failing degree is **four if the monoid is a group and three otherwise**. This is already undecidable with every relator of the form $w=1$: use the group-recognition theorem for finite special monoid presentations, supplying each relator as a birth and a death. The restriction to a nonempty alphabet costs nothing since the empty alphabet presents the trivial group. Thus undirected local relations with only one spatial site of definition suffice for undecidability of the exact spectrum. [Narendran–Ó'Dúnlaing–Otto, *It is undecidable whether a finite special string-rewriting system presents a group*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X(91)90040-9)

The general ordinary cases and the Gray classification with spatially mixed 3-rules or unrestricted higher attachments still require further arguments.

### The raw criterion

Let $b_1,\ldots,b_s$ be the right letters of $S$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_t$ the left letters of $T$, in temporal order. Choose a shuffle $M$ of these two fixed lists. Split $S,M$ at the $b$'s, giving left segments $u_0,\ldots,u_s$ and $v_0,\ldots,v_s$. Split $M,T$ at the $a$'s, giving right segments $m_0,\ldots,m_t$ and $n_0,\ldots,n_t$. Then a raw filler exists if and only if some $M$ admits partners satisfying
$$
\begin{aligned}
u_j d_{j+1}&\le_L d_j v_j &&(0\le j\le s),\\
e_i m_i&\le_R n_i e_{i+1} &&(0\le i\le t).
\end{aligned}
$$
Products are temporal concatenations. The two exterior partners in each row are empty paths. The internal $d_j$ goes from the left state at $b_j$ in $S$ to that in $M$. The internal $e_i$ goes from the right state at $a_i$ in $T$ to that in $M$. Thus each inequality compares parallel paths, even when the successive spatial paths differ in length.

$$
F(c)=
\begin{cases}
 c & c\le h,\\

 c-l+k & h+l<c .
\end{cases}
$$
Compose these functions along $p$ to get $F_p$. For $q$ measure offsets from the other temporal end and transport suffix lengths by the same formula, giving $G_q$. For every cut of $S$, initially mark the left prefix before it and the right suffix after it. Throughout the derivation every transported marked left letter precedes every transported marked right letter. A left rewrite meeting the marked prefix has no intervening right letter and its output can occupy its position; a birth at the end of the prefix stays outside. A birth strictly inside has a later marked letter. The mirror argument handles the right rewrites, and a native exchange preserves the order. This is the two-cut invariant of Response 142 applied to *each* source cut.

Run $p$ first, keeping the source right letters as separators. For each nonempty redex, move every separator strictly inside it to its far end by native exchanges, preserving separator order. Next run $q$ with the left letters of $M$ as separators, using the temporally mirrored procedure. Internal left separators move to the near end of the right redex, also by native exchanges. Call the result $U$. For left letter $a_i$ let $k$ be the number of right letters *after* it in $M$. Exactly $G_q(k)$ right letters follow it in $U$. When $k>0$, take the first of those $k$ source right letters and consider the cut immediately before it in $S$. If $c$ left letters precede this cut, then $F_p(c)\ge i$ by construction of $M$. Its marked right suffix has length $k$. The invariant in the original derivation therefore places at least $G_q(k)$ right letters after $a_i$ in $T$. The same bound holds for $k=0$ since $G_q(0)=0$. The projections of $U$ and $T$ agree literally. Move the left letters in their given order, each leftwards past right letters until its target position is reached. The inequalities just proved guarantee these are all native moves. This gives a first phase with fixed right letters, then a second phase with fixed left letters, including the final exchanges.

**Eliminating the separators.** In the first phase record as $d_j$ the letters crossing $b_j$, in chronological order. In segment $j$, prefix the current word by the part of $d_j$ already sent across its left separator and suffix it by the part of $d_{j+1}$ still to arrive across its right separator. This combined word is typed: a transfer changes the spatial state at the separator by exactly the transferred letter. Transfers leave the combined word identical and local rewrites give forward inequalities. Its initial and final values are exactly the first row. Conversely execute the first row from $j=s$ down to $0$. After the incoming $d_{j+1}$ has arrived, apply the inequality and transfer its output prefix $d_j$ across the preceding right separator. This leaves $v_j$ in place. For the second phase reverse the temporal reading and exchange the two colours. Transfers now record the letters in reverse chronological order in the original reading. Restoring temporal order gives exactly the second row, executable from $i=0$ up to $t$. Empty transferred words and nullary local rules require no exceptional case. This proves both directions.

### Consequences for Q2

Join disjoint finite Gray computads $P,Q$ by one new edge from a chosen vertex of $P$ to a chosen vertex of $Q$, without further declarations. On any interchange surface the joined context is conservative through degree three **if and only if** both components are conservative through degree three and at least one of the following holds.

- Every positioned elementary step on a spatial path ending at the chosen vertex of $P$ has a left adjoint in its local path preorder.
- Every positioned elementary step on a spatial path starting at the chosen vertex of $Q$ has a right adjoint there.

Here an adjoint means the two directed inequalities of Response 142, for the positioned step at its actual spatial paths. To verify the criterion use the elementary returns of Response 2. A path lies in a single component or crosses the new edge once. Internal exchanges in a crossing path lift from the corresponding component by stationary whiskering. Conversely a return in a component cannot use the new edge, since its spatial path stays in that component. At a mixed exchange, take the two steps alone in its temporal window. The only possible intermediate shuffles for its reverse $a b\to b a$ are $a b$ and $b a$. The two rows reduce respectively to the right and the left adjunction alternatives of Response 142, now with *all* directed local moves on the relevant spatial paths available. Every ordered pair of the indicated left and right steps is realizable across the joining edge. Hence failure of both universal alternatives gives a single mixed counterexample by choosing one failing step on each side. This also explains why testing only unwhiskered generating labels would not suffice as an argument on general components.

For an individual boundary the shuffle and the partners can be found together. With finite tables for the local path categories modulo mutual reachability, scan a lattice path with coordinates $(i,j)$ counting target left letters and source right letters already used. Store the left coordinate at the last right letter, the right coordinate at the last left letter, and the two current partners. At a right step, the intervening target left substring is $v_j$. Choose the next typed left partner, test row one at $j$, and record the new left cut. At a left step do the mirror test on the intervening source right substring $m_i$ with row two. At the end test both final segments against the exterior identities. These transitions are precisely the inequalities above. With $D,E$ local arrow classes this uses at most $(t+1)^2(s+1)^2DE$ states and at most $D+E$ choices per state. Substring products can be tabulated in advance.

In the finite single-edge presentations of Response 142 this decision also works under the *promise* of finite local quotients, without supplied tables. Enumerate finite ordered categories on the given objects, assignments of generating changes satisfying the declared comparisons, and a parallel representative word for each arrow evaluating to that arrow. Require actual local derivations in both directions between the representatives of identities, generators and products and their prescribed spellings, and a forward local derivation between the representatives of each table comparison. All are finitely many certificates and their searches can be dovetailed. Satisfaction sends every local derivation to a table inequality. Conversely every word is mutually reachable with its representative by induction on length, so the comparisons with certified derivations reflect the order. The true finite quotients have precisely such certificates. This does not assume a bound on raw witness lengths.

**Validation.** Run `python3 tools/semistrict_surface_shuffle_interpolation.py`. The lattice search agrees with independent exhaustive mixed rewriting on 133,956 typed judgments from two acyclic local graphs (14,651 raw-positive), including local splits, merges and distinct parallel labels. On two idempotent monoids with optional births and deaths it agrees on 3,600 judgments (2,167 positive). For the latter direct search, endpoints have length at most three and width eight suffices: in the first phase the stationary right letters, all source and target left letters, and at most two one-letter partners bound the width by $|S|+|T|+2$. The same count holds in the second phase. Each local inequality is realized by contracting each nonempty power to one letter, applying the indicated birth or death if necessary, then expanding to the required output; this never exceeds the larger of the local input and output lengths. With `--agda-dir DIR`, the checker also writes `GrayShuffleInterpolation.agda`. Running `agda --safe -i src -i DIR DIR/GrayShuffleInterpolation.agda` checks a raw filler from $B A B$ to $A' B' B$ with a declared update on each side, a native exchange, and fixed exterior event. The all-dimensional cases of Q1 and Q2 beyond the previously proved classes remain open. [Shuffle decision and independent rewrite search](../../../tools/semistrict_surface_shuffle_interpolation.py)

**Pure packet inclusion at a partial reversal.** For a full reversal, reduced words modulo distant commutations give the elements of $B(n,2)$. Felsner and Weil prove that inclusion of the triple inversion sets is equivalent to a sequence of directed single-triple flips. Their Theorem 1 applies in every width. For any simple braid extend both readings by the same positive sorting suffix to the full reversal. A triple using a suffix crossing has the same packet order at both ends: the same pairs lie before the cut, the suffix order is fixed, and the two possible packet orders are reversals of each other. The expanded reading is still simple: an external pair crosses only in its one block exchange, and an internal pair crosses only at its assigned update. Its final permutation depends only on the original end order and per-strand counts.

A triple from three distinct blocks contributes the packet bit for those original events. A complete triple from two blocks must contain the central strand and a crossing helper of one block, and one strand of the other block. Its packet bit is one precisely when that other block precedes the update at its checkpoint. To see the sign, if the marked block is initially first, the internal pair is lexicographically first and is executed last precisely after the external block crossing. If the marked block is initially second, the internal pair is lexicographically last and is executed first precisely before the external crossing. In both cases the recorded bit is membership in the same prefix. For block pairs that do not exchange this membership is constant. Three strands of a single block never make a complete triple. Hence the two displayed inclusions give packet inclusion in the entire expanded simple braid.

Apply the pure result to the expanded words. Project a word along the flip chain by remembering every central–central crossing as an original exchange and a central strand's crossing with its own helper as the private update it indexes. Erase the remaining crossings. On each central strand the helpers meet it in the prescribed order, since the helpers never cross one another. A distant commutation of retained operations is strict disjoint exchange. A three-central flip gives a native cube. A flip on the two strands for one update and another central strand gives the native mixed prism, directed toward the larger prefix by the sign calculation. Every other flip has at most one retained operation and projects to an identity. The erased pure central path remains an executable positive spelling of the original braid; the updates preserve both spatial ports. ### A comparison that commutes with forgetting a port

Use a finite set of marks with one mark for **each wire** and a separate singleton mark for **each use**. The trace of a wire mark consists of the wire and its incident uses, when present. For a subset of the marks retain the selected wires, all their incident uses, and every use selected by its singleton. Thus a use retained solely by its singleton has two empty port lists. Restriction to a smaller subset composes literally. In particular one can forget an input port while keeping the use and all its outputs. We need a single comparison $F:C\to C$ on the original network compatible, in the homotopy theory of diagrams over cuts, with such restrictions from larger networks.

Here are the checks to apply the construction of Responses 86, 99 and 104 with these marks. At a cut a wire mark is present only on its live wire. At a batch it is either absent, on a stationary wire, or on its incident jumping site. Its two incident sites cannot jump simultaneously because the wire orders them. A singleton is present just at its jumping site. Replacing a site by a port block leaves each surviving exterior edge of a complete graph unchanged. Each new internal edge is one tested in the ordered configuration at that end of the site. Marks that disappear at this expansion impose no edge constraint there. Forgetting marks restricts these same ordered graphs, omitting a site direction entirely exactly when the use disappears. This gives the constrained cube diagram with face maps commuting with deletion. It also gives the pure-to-cut inclusions using the live wire marks.

In an interval each nonempty part of a mark's trace is connected. In particular, if both uses at the ends of a wire occur, the wire joins them inside the interval. At a spatial split of a term the slots run independently. Each present trace therefore belongs to one slot, and every occupied slot has a wire or use carrying a mark. This remains true after restriction, including when only a singleton survives. On each frontier the section for a split juxtaposes the graphs on its blocks, imposing the specified signed exterior edges; its order homotopy to the original graph commutes with expanding sites by the preceding face check. The test at an endpoint block of a use takes place wholly within its slot. These are exactly the hypotheses giving the block product on **every** restriction, hence the trivial matching fibration at a split in Response 99. Intersections of the deletion indices are still intersections of subsets of the mark set, even when different subsets retain an identical presentation. At a bare rule the induced map of published presentations retains the rule with the inherited order on the remaining ports. A deleted wire is an identity scalar, so insertion and disc reduction give precisely that shortened block at each end. If the rule disappears its two blocks have disappeared and its image is the higher identity. The bare-rule assignment in the diagram is the corresponding characteristic arrow, including the arrow at a site with two empty ends. On a split symbol record the bound for marks in different occupied slots and use the bounds of the arguments inside each slot. **One can bound the number of ports at interior ranks while preserving the failure spectrum of the entire context through any prescribed degree.** Fix either kernel, a finite computad $D$, a degree bound $d$, and any set $R\subseteq\{2,\ldots,d\}$ with no consecutive entries. $$

$$
  \{j\le d:\text{conservativity fails in }D\text{ in degree }j\}
   =\{j\le d:\text{conservativity fails in }E\text{ in degree }j\}.
$$
This includes failures at types involving the auxiliary declarations of $E$. One can take $R$ to consist of all even ranks or all odd ranks above one. In degree $r$ this adds a forward comparison $u\to a$ and two comparisons $a\to u$. All three are equivalences in the full attachment. All further data have degree greater than $r$, with finitely many declarations through every fixed cap. The inclusion of the base into the full attachment is a raw weak equivalence: in ordinary realization the inclusion of the first pole is the suspension of the endpoint equivalence; in Gray realization take $n-1$ ordinary suspensions and then one enriched suspension. We have obtained clause (i) using only published units and $T$. [Reconstruction at a common source](#researcher-response-16)

For clause (ii), first use the just-proved equality on the *generic* arity to convert the two faces of its head to the same word. Published endo-coherence removal gives the identity there; applying the actual substitution gives the claimed equation. All top reassociations belong already to clause (i) for $A$, by the raw-parallel triple of composable discs and substitution. These two inclusions prove both middle equalities, in arbitrary ambient contexts and also inside formal head types. For a Gray model the same argument for (i) needs only equality with the padded core for its binary operations and strictly associative top products. For (ii) it suffices to require the identity value at agreed generic face functions with identity strict tag, on *all* arities, as in Response 51: the common strict faces of such a Gray head in a pasting arity have only the identity endomorphism. This gives a condition for proving Q1 without choosing lower-cut associators in the proposed model.

### Why published insertion gives a genuinely stronger proof obligation

There is an exact rank-one normal form for the middle ordinary theory on any computad. At fixed object ends use lists of atoms. An atom is a generating edge or a node containing an ordered tuple of at least three composable nonempty lists. An identity is the empty list. At an unbiased path head discard empty arguments. Zero remaining lists give an identity, one gives that list, two concatenate, and three or more give a singleton list containing the node on those arguments. This follows in the theory by pruning, disc and endo removal, and binary top associativity. Conversely evaluate into the model with these vertices and paths and a unique higher cell on each parallel boundary. The displayed path operations respect pruning at every empty slot and return the generator on a disc. Binary concatenation is associative and unital. In degree one all ordinary heads are path or point heads, since their generic ends are objects. Higher operations and equations are forced at the already verified boundaries. Each original higher declaration therefore has an interpretation. Reading each list back by binary concatenation and each node by its unbiased head proves the normal form is complete, including for paths with repeated edges.

On three successive edges, the three-input path head consequently differs from either binary bracketing, whereas published insertion identifies it with a binary composite with one inner binary composite. This gives the last strict inclusion, using the containment of unit pruning in insertion and of the binary $\{A,U\}$ laws in insertion. The two binary bracketings themselves are distinct under published units alone: neither has an identity input, a disc head or an endo head, so they have distinct unit normal forms. This gives the first strict inclusion. The distinction concerns conversion; all three terms have the same old path endpoints.

On 22,752 raw binary words it checked commutation with both literal faces. Among the words with the same raw type and flattened core there were 14,969 additional representatives; every group had a single tree modulo top reassociation. There were 72 groups in which omitting the type test would have conflated different such trees. Rice's strict-unit checker verified 404 equalities to the pruned writings. Six mixed comparisons in ranks two through four and the three-input path comparison separated strict-unit conversion from insertion. The rank-one model also passed 7,737 direct pruning checks. These results reduce the equations needed for the joint model. A comparison returning inhabitants from such a model at arbitrary old boundaries, or a counterexample there, is still needed for the universal $\{A,U\}$ cases of Q1.

For sufficiency one can fit any placed rule to the current tuple by putting the remaining group labels in the outer unary context; commuting cycles make its change independent of that choice. **Three tests.**

1. For each legal signed exchange $h\to k$, permuting coordinates by its transposition must carry $M_h$ onto $M_k$.
2. For each rule with crossings, strip its two crossing words and read the label difference on its input slots. This difference must belong to $M_h$ at the rule's own starting history.
3. Cover every bare spatial triple by a projected mixed reverse cube, as in Response 171. To qualify, both the label difference and its negative must belong to $M_h$ at the cube rule's history.

Any transported generator in test 1 has a signed surface proof at a zero-crossing boundary: conjugate the placed rule by the exchange and its signed inverse. Failure of membership gives an actual raw-negative witness there. Test 2 is necessary by stripping the common structural braid. Assuming these tests, every raw or surface step with a given input history changes the normalized decorations by an element of $M_h$: extend the raw zero-crossing realization to the larger spatial and temporal context, then transport along the prefix by test 1. At a bare cube return the total increment is zero. A sum of increments from a monoid is zero only if each summand is a unit of that monoid. The literal transition from $212$ to $121$ must therefore be supplied by a rule in test 3. Conversely the three conditions let a raw proof first realize the full joint label increment at the input, then perform positive Artin moves using the reversibly decorated cubes. This covers any parallel old writings by the fixed-hom fitting in Response 171. Tests 2 and 3 are finite integer membership and the finite gap-dictionary calculation of Response 52. An exchange wholly before or after its temporal interval leaves the placement available. An exchange inside can be tested on the original rule history at its bare spatial path. The remaining exchange involves its first or last event and one extra event immediately outside. Drop the unused temporal prefix and suffix. At the spatial slice between the rule interval and that extra event, mark two intervals: the whole rule subpath and the extra event's incident subpath. If the extra event comes first these are the rule input and the event output; in the other order they are the rule output and the event input. Trim stationary wires outside their span. Intersecting or touching intervals have just finitely many relative offsets; check the shared edge letters and vertices, reconstruct the two temporal pieces, and test each executable exchange. This includes intervals of length zero.

For separated intervals there is a gap path $g$ between them, untouched by every event in the test. Let $L$ be the maximum initial spatial path length of a crossing-free rule with nonzero difference, or zero if there is none. Keep short $g$ exactly up to length $2L$, and for longer $g$ keep its two length-$L$ ends and endpoints. This suffices to compute every generator row of $M$ on the exchanged history. A rule placed across both sides of a long gap would have to contain all the untouched gap wires in its initial subpath, which has length at most $L$. A placement confined to one side can inspect at most $L$ adjacent gap letters. Its temporal interval, relative spatial offsets and vector contribution are unchanged by replacing the middle of the gap. One can also see this from the subpath match at the first slice of a candidate interval: throughout the fragment an outside wire cannot enter or leave a placed subdiagram. Enumerate a representative of each realizable path class by a finite automaton tracking the current vertex, the two truncated ends and the length capped at $2L+1$. Empty gaps have already been included among touching intervals. A positive check in the trimmed chart extends by whiskering; any failure there is itself an old counterexample. This proves finiteness even on a cyclic generating edge graph, including when the extra event creates or consumes its entire local path.

**Sharpness of the extra slot.** At a single scalar with one invertible unary loop, supply the bare reverse cube and one crossing-free rule adding one unit to each of $m\ge2$ consecutive occurrences. Through temporal width $m$ all comparisons reflect: below $m$ the rule has no effect, and at $m$ its all-ones vector is permutation-invariant and available raw. On $m+1$ occurrences the surface transports that vector to a set of $m$ slots omitting an interior slot. At zero crossings a raw move can add only one of the two consecutive length-$m$ vectors. Total increment $m$ forces exactly one application, so the requested vector is impossible. The theorem bounds temporal width of a missing old comparison by the largest of three, the maximum mixed-rule width and one plus the maximum nontrivial crossing-free rule width.

## Researcher Response 173

**Deciding reflection at every old 4-type in the mixed commuting-label class of Response 172 is NP-complete, measured in the explicit finite presentation.** Failure somewhere is coNP-complete. The lower bound already holds on one scalar with a bare reverse cube, one crossing-guarded rule of width two, and unguarded unary rules at width one. For the upper bound even joint, spatially guarded zero-crossing rules on arbitrary finite 2-bases are allowed. In particular a positive answer has a polynomial-size certificate that can be checked without a monoid-membership oracle. [All-boundary criterion](#researcher-response-172)

**Polynomially many spatial gaps.** Let $D$ contain the empty word and all contiguous substrings of the initial spatial paths of nonzero crossing-free rules. Its size is at most one plus the sum of the squared path lengths. For a separated gap $g$ in Response 172 retain its endpoints, whether $g\in D$, its longest prefix in $D$, and its longest suffix in $D$. If $g\in D$ this retains the entire word. Otherwise no nonzero placement can inspect the entire gap: any such inspection would put the whole untouched word inside that rule's initial spatial path. A placement touching only one side can inspect gap letters only in a prefix or suffix lying in $D$. Existence of every required match is thus determined by the two longest matches. Conversely, for two gaps with identical data, copy the same placement on the same side, translating any offsets on the far side by the length difference. Its literal path and vertices still match; the ordered occurrence slots and the contributed vector agree. This includes a rule initially extending into the gap while all its events occur on one side. A placement with events on both sides would have to inspect the entire gap.

There is a deterministic left-to-right automaton for this data. Its prefix remains live while the entire word belongs to $D$; on the first failed extension freeze the prefix. For the new suffix take the longest suffix of the previous suffix followed by the new letter that belongs to $D$. Indeed the prefix of any nonempty newly matching suffix, with its last letter removed, was a matching suffix one step earlier. Include the current graph vertex to enforce composability. From each fixed start vertex there are at most $2|V||D|^2$ states. Breadth-first search supplies polynomially many representatives of polynomial length. All touching and intersecting interval tests, transport signs and guarded rule tests of Response 172 also have polynomially many choices. At a fixed representative, listing all monoid rows takes polynomial time by checking temporal starts and spatial offsets. The bare-triple dictionary coverage test is polynomial: for each colour triple use the two tries of explicitly listed gap paths and reachability in the finite generating graph, as in Response 52.

Guess nonnegative integer coefficients for every required inclusion. For reverse cube coverage it suffices to guess a covering subset of the candidates and give coefficients for the reverse increments of the selected candidates; no proof of nonmembership for any omitted candidate is needed. An integer solution to each nonnegative linear system has polynomial bit length in its matrix and target whenever it exists. Thus the total guessed certificate has polynomial size. Each rule's structural braid-preserving hypothesis can itself be checked in polynomial time: write each positive letter as a simple permutation braid and move an atom from the right factor into the left whenever the latter remains simple. Each transfer increases the sum of all prefix lengths of the factorization by one; this sum is at most the square of the word length. At termination the left-weighted factors form the unique positive greedy normal form. The executable verifier uses these permutation factors and integer vector equalities. [Integer certificate bound](https://ii.uni.wroc.pl/~aje/WordEq2015/papers/Papadimitriou.pdf) · [Greedy braid normal form](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.07788)

**Lower bound.** Given an EXACT COVER instance on universe $U$, take one scalar and one commuting invertible unary loop $d_u$ for each element. For every input set $S$ add the unguarded unary rule from the empty decoration to the product of the $d_u$ for $u\in S$. Add the bare reverse cube. On two scalars add one declaration taking a single crossing to the same crossing preceded by one $d_u$ for every $u\in U$ on the first occurrence. All spatial contexts are empty. By Response 171 the presentation reflects in degree four exactly when the all-ones vector is a nonnegative sum of the incidence vectors of the sets. Such a sum uses each element exactly once, giving an exact cover, and an exact cover provides the sum. This is a polynomial reduction even with the commutations written explicitly. Equivalently, at the particular zero-crossing old type obtained by stripping the guard, the surface is always inhabited and raw inhabitation is equivalent to exact cover. [Karp's EXACT COVER problem](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~gasarch/BLOGPAPERS/Karp.pdf)

At a prefix, check the actual temporal interval and spatial subpath. The edge weight is the rule's decoration difference on the corresponding input occurrences, zero for a native move. Each left or right transition replaces two neighbouring symbols, and a stationary transition replaces one. On accepting, enter a deterministic sweep that clears the tape and returns the head to the first cell in a fixed final state. A well-formed initial configuration reaches the prescribed equal-length final configuration exactly on acceptance. This uses one finite alphabet and one fixed finite list of rules, independent of the input length. Applying the protected encoding gives the claimed fixed context. Write $C=\mathfrak F(\Gamma)$, and write a bar for its projection to the ordinary free strict category $F$ on the declarations with their projected attaching maps. At any cut $j$ the exact composition formula is

### A machine that can fail only at five

Adjoin r from V to U, X from U to V, loops B,D at V and loops K,C,L,E, the counter letters a,b, and the program states at U. In a segment between r's, a positive path crosses forward at most once, either by j or by X. Add five separately named 4-rules, in chronological word notation:
```
take          K j           → L start E X
release       L done E X    → C j
observe       j B           → j D
bare-observe  B             → D
bare-close    K             → C
```
The remaining rules at U implement the deterministic machine on a word L aⁿ q bᵐ E. Increments insert a counter next to the state, positive tests consume it, and zero tests inspect the adjacent end marker. After halt drain both counters before entering done. No machine rule consumes an end marker permanently or uses X, K, C, B, D or r. The branch from the displayed take reaches the displayed release exactly for a halting blank-input machine. The generators and rules are effective in the finite program. [Counter machine convention and universality](#researcher-response-177)

The return r handles degree three. To prove degree four for *every* input, start with any projected substring derivation between positive old paths. Mark each block L start E X created by a new take. Until its release the entire block remains contiguous and only its own machine instructions can change its interior. Its sentinel tests face inwards, no external instruction can cross its L or X, and no nested take is possible inside it. In the intermediate computation represent each such live block by its original K. Its acquisition and private instructions then do nothing, and its release executes bare-close. Remember its private instructions. Every other rewrite on unmarked letters lifts at its represented position: the machine and bare rules act in just one state of the graph, an observer can always use bare-observe, and an unmarked release has its literal U-side word followed by X. At the target, a surviving marked block contains X, so it is the unique forward crossing in its segment. Its representing K now occurs immediately before j in the positive lift, where take followed by the recorded private instructions restores the actual block. Restore all such blocks; they lie in distinct segments. Deleting j has at most one positive lift at fixed endpoints: the types of successive visible letters force each intervening j, including at the exterior ends. This proves reflection at the written degree-four faces, including paths with pre-existing X's, machine states, or end markers. [Projected degree-four reachability](#researcher-response-185)

If the machine halts, compare two 4-pastes from K j B to C j D. One applies observe first, then take, the machine run and release. The other performs the very same left computation first, then observe. Their input j feeds different vertices, so they are distinct raw diagrams. After erasure the full K-to-C computation is disjoint from the one B-to-D vertex. They are equal projected diagrams. The individual test gives exactly the asserted failure.

If the machine runs forever, a newly taken block cannot release, even if the old source contained other machine data. In each fixed r-segment a live j can therefore occur over just one time interval. It may be present initially, or appear at the release of a pre-existing X. A take consumes it, and no later release is possible in that segment. The only vertex preserving a live j and using it is observe. It can occur at most once in the segment: it changes the first V-loop B to D, no rule creates B or consumes D, and a V-loop always retains its position in the V-suffix. The immutable r wires and planar order identify each segment in the erased diagram. Reconstruct its j incidence by joining the unique initial j or release output to the unique observe if present, then to the unique take or final j, omitting unused portions when there is no j. These are all ports of this colour, and their positions on their named vertices are prescribed. Thus the erased diagram and original boundaries determine the entire raw diagram. Faithfulness holds at every positive old path, also when a pre-existing malformed machine block releases. This proves conservativity in the nonhalting case. Reduction from blank-input nonhalting proves the promised lower bound.

### A finite-capacity machine in binary rules

Use U-loops for work letters, a bridge X from U to V, the native j and its declared return r, and observer loops B,D at V. Start with the rules
```
take           K j     → H X
grow           Z H     → H T₀
launch         H T₀    → L start
release        A X     → C j
observe        j B     → j D
bare-observe   B       → D
bare-close     K       → C
```
T₀ is a blank two-bit tape cell. After borrowing n+1 copies of Z to its left, take followed by the grows and launch gives L start T₀ⁿ X. The two counters are the numbers of set bits on tracks 0 and 1. For an increment, scan right across cells whose selected bit is set; at the first clear bit set it and turn left in the destination return state. An increment lacking space stops. For a test, scan across clear cells; on a set bit clear it and turn left in the positive destination state. At X take the zero branch. Each scan move swaps a state and a tape cell, the bit-changing move replaces a state-cell pair, and the zero branch replaces a state next to X. A returning state crosses tape cells to the left and resumes its instruction at L. These rules simulate precisely the two counters with capacity n on each track.

At halt sweep right clearing the remaining tape, turn at X, and return to L over blanks. Replace L back by A T₀. The rule A T₀ → Z A releases each borrowed space to the left; finish with release. Thus the complete left computation is Zⁿ⁺¹ K j →* Zⁿ⁺¹ C j. A fresh acquisition can release exactly when its blank launch halts within its chosen finite capacity. An unrestricted machine halts on blank exactly when it succeeds at some capacity, since a halting run visits only finitely many counter values. Every rule preserves raw length. Upon erasing j give K,C weight two and every other letter weight one. Every projected rule preserves this weight, including acquisition and release. All raw rule sides have width one or two and stay nonempty upon erasure.

### Global reflection at the old boundaries

The virtualization argument at four must account for borrowing space from outside a new block. In a projected derivation mark each new H X from take. Mark each Z it absorbs by grow. From launch to halt only internal instructions can act on the marked block: L and X face inwards, and the machine head remains between them. During shrink retain the marks on newly emitted leading Z's. These Z's cannot participate in any external rule: only grow consumes Z, from immediately to the left of H, and to the right of the emitted Z's is the same block's A. Outside actions are disjoint except for the explicit borrow before launch. A tagged block with k borrowed positions is represented by Zᵏ K throughout, including its partially completed shrink. A borrow absorbs the adjacent unmarked Z into this representation without changing the represented word. Release substitutes bare-close on its K and leaves its k copies of Z. Every other unmarked rule lifts at its typed location, using bare-observe for observe. In particular a test at an unmarked X, or an unmarked release there, has a literal positive raw window. In a positive final target each surviving block has the unique X in its r-segment; its represented K is immediately before j. Execute its take, replay all its recorded grows and private steps using its retained Z's, and stop at its actual final phase. Distinct surviving blocks occupy distinct segments. This constructs the raw route to the given old target. It covers unfinished scans, pre-existing tape data and releases of older blocks.

On a nonhalting machine no freshly taken block can release at any capacity. As in Response 187, in each r-segment the j incidence therefore forms at most one interval, with at most one guarded observer. No step creates a B, consumes a D, or changes the order of the V-loops. All additional scan, turn, borrow and shrink vertices are j-free. Hence the original parallel diagrams are determined by their projections. On a halting machine choose sufficient space n and move the very same guarded observer from before the complete acquisition/computation/release to after it, at the old source Zⁿ⁺¹ K j B. The two diagrams differ on the input j and coincide after erasure. This proves the reduction under all the stated promises.

In particular **there is no computable bound, as a function of the presentation, on the source-word length needed to detect a degree-five failure** in this binary family. If there were a bound N, test the deterministic bounded-counter machine at every capacity through N. A failing source of length at most N entails the release of a freshly acquired block in some reading: without one, the unique-interval reconstruction proves faithfulness there. That block can borrow only positions of its fixed-length word and witnesses halting within capacity N. This finite test would decide unrestricted blank-input halting. Thus increasing a fixed word-length cutoff cannot give a complete global recognition algorithm even though each pair of supplied traces has an exact decision.

### Computing both tests

At four first compare the two projected planar diagrams in each column. For identical projections write s,t for the lifted local 2-chains. A strict filling amounts exactly to a nonnegative integral solution of ∂z=t−s. Its possible terms are p tensor f and e tensor q, for left/right polygons p,q and edges e,f. Integral solutions exist before enforcing positivity by contractibility. All differ by the boundary of a unique integer array x indexed by polygon pairs. Each edge in an occurrence complex has at most one creating and one consuming polygon. Consequently each prism coefficient has the form
\[
                 z_0 + x_{\rm creator} - x_{\rm consumer},
\]
with the polygon on the other side fixed, and absent indices interpreted as zero. This sign is positive on both sorts of prisms because the degree of p is two in ∂(p tensor q). Nonnegativity is an ordinary system of difference constraints. It has an integer solution exactly when its graph has no negative cycle, and shortest-path potentials give a filling.

For an explicit particular solution, keep the initial path and omit the last new output edge of each polygon from the column graph. The remaining edges form a spanning tree: on each attachment all new internal vertices join the tree by the retained part of its output path. For each polygon on either side route a signed tree path between its old positions in the opposite complex. These coefficients solve the polygon-vertex and vertex-polygon equations. The residual difference on edge-tensor-edge is a 2-cycle. For each fixed left edge its row is a 1-cycle on the right. Expand it in the right polygon boundaries by eliminating the distinguished last output edge of each polygon in reverse attachment order. This expansion is unique. Subtract the resulting coefficients from the edge-tensor-polygon entries, since the right boundary there has sign minus. The correction does not change the vertex-tensor-polygon equation: the left boundary of the residual is zero and the right polygon boundaries are independent. This supplies the required particular solution. At five the difference of two valid parallel prism chains is the boundary of a unique polygon-pair array, found by the same triangular elimination. Its entries must all be nonnegative. All graph sizes, integer operations and bit lengths here are polynomial in the explicit readings or tableau input; the bound does not assume rules of fixed width.

To prove necessity on a pair, order parallel arrows in the strict braided monoidal groupoid of coloured lists as follows. At each two-strand multiset use the indicated difference monoid. At higher weights allow all comparisons. At weights zero and one there is only the identity braid at a given object. This is a preorder preserved by composition, tensor and the braiding constraints. In weight two a tensor either adds an empty list or combines two singletons, and pre- and postcomposition add the same crossing sum to both sides. One can therefore transport any prescribed 2-source and 2-target to chosen product writings and represent any intervening braid path there, with inverse paths and raw comparisons for cancellation. More explicitly, the 1-poles lie in the point and can first be moved to its identity; the two 2-faces can then be moved within their configuration component. Concatenating such steps realizes every nonnegative sum of the recorded differences. This proves the first assertion.

If every pair monoid is all of $\mathbb Z$, both signs of a half twist on an identical pair and of a full twist on a distinct pair can be inserted or contracted. Place these comparisons on adjacent strands in a longer product, rebracketing in the scalar base. They kill in both directions every loop in the coloured braid groupoid. Indeed the pure braid group is generated by full twists on two strands transported to adjacent position: forget the last point, whose fibre is the plane punctured at the other points, and use its meridians inductively. Moving a pair adjacent in the groupoid and transporting its half twist back realizes each needed transposition. For a split of rank $n$, $j\ge l$: the two new slots lie in the same group, and their inner binary value is exactly their concatenation. ### Scheduling actual prisms

The coefficients z(p,f) for a fixed private p form a positive path in Q from its source gap to its target gap. This is the polygon-vertex equation. The coefficients z(e,q) for fixed q form a positive path in P by the vertex-polygon equation. Each coefficient is zero or one. Think of the old square at (e,f) as available exactly when these live wires cross.

* A left prism (p,f) consumes the squares at the input edges of p paired with f and produces the squares at its output edges paired with f. The p-gap traverses f.
* A right prism (e,q) consumes squares at e paired with the **output** edges of q and produces squares at e paired with its input edges. The q-gap traverses e.

Order P by any total extension of its strong basis order. Order Q by a strong order of its planar diagram **read with polygon directions reversed but edge directions unchanged**. This exists by rebuilding the same occurrence diagram from its final cut and attaching the reversed polygons as in Response 189. Process the required pairs in lexicographic product order. Every producer of a square precedes the square position and every consumer follows it in that order. All previous moves required along a polygon's own gap path also precede the current one, because the spatial edge directions were retained in both factors. Thus at each move the polygon is at the source gap of the indicated edge, and every required input square is available: its initial multiplicity plus its earlier productions is at least its total consumptions by the square boundary equation.

These are actual local redexes. For a left prism, f visits the full consecutive input path of p; there can be no extra visits in the middle, as that would be a nonempty path from a vertex of P to itself. After each such crossing the left wire feeds p directly: another crossing would give a nonempty backwards path in Q from the source of f to the current p-gap, the very same vertex. For a right prism the reciprocal argument gives the entire output path of q on e in backwards order, with the outgoing right wires coming directly from q. Thus the indicated swaps and polygon form the native negative prism face. They can be made consecutive in a reading. In the left case all exterior entrances are at or before the last swap and all exits are at or after that swap. In the right case the first swap has this property. Contract the block, sort the wire dependencies, then expand. Firing it therefore gives a true 3-reading with the asserted square updates. On completion all square data, marks and shared occurrences match the target. This proves sufficiency at four at the written boundaries by [positive-attachment lifting](#researcher-response-8).

A raw prism paste at fixed old ends is determined as a strict cell by its counts z. In a sequential prism reading, exchange an adjacent inversion relative to the scheduling order. The later move could not depend on a square produced by the earlier one, or on the earlier move advancing the same gap, since all such dependencies are in scheduling order. Both moves were therefore enabled, with distinct private polygons and no common consumed square (a square consumed by the first cannot be consumed by the immediately following move). Their redexes are disjoint. They can be made whole blocks together: any dependency between such blocks strictly orders the swaps separating their entrances from their exits as above. Joint contraction thus preserves acyclicity. Independent replacements in this reading commute by strict interchange. Sorting identifies all readings with that z.

### Exposing one polygon-pair generator and commuting its uses

Suppose w≥0 between two prism pastes. Add its polygon-pair units one at a time, processing creators before consumers in the **original** two planar polygon orders. At an increment (p,q), the current z contains all its negative facets, namely (p,f) for the inputs f of q and (e,q) for the inputs e of p. Outgoing facets only increase. This gives feasible intermediate chains.

To realize one increment, substitute **one block** for these negative prism moves in the scheduler. Put it at product position (p,q). It consumes exactly the rectangle input(p) × output(q) of squares and produces output(p) × input(q). Its p-gap traverses the input path of q and its q-gap the input path of p. These are consecutive subpaths of their respective gap routes. The same order works: consumed squares are below the block in both coordinates, produced squares above it, and other moves on either gap precede or follow the whole subpath. At the block, all consumed squares therefore exist and the two gaps are at the initial vertices of those paths.

In the actual planar reading q now feeds the right wires directly into this rectangle, whose left wires feed p directly on exit. This follows from the two directed wire paths and the gap tests exactly as for a single prism. The rectangle, q and p are the common 2-source of the polygon-pair tensor generator. To expose them, let e be the last input edge of p and f the last output edge of q in their path orders. Every exterior entrance into this diagram is at or before the crossing (e,f), and every exit is at or after it. Indeed the left wires enter on f, the right wires start at q, the right wires leave on e, and all left outputs come from p. Thus joint contraction gives a consecutive realization. Inside it the native 4-atom p tensor q changes the negative prism paste to the positive one. The count uniqueness just proved identifies the required old prism pastes. For clarity, equality in degree six also requires comparing *uses* of these atoms. A single contextual use at a given z and (p,q) is unique as a strict 4-cell. Sorting this augmented sequence works just as for prism sequences. A genuine inversion cannot share an advancing polygon with the block: the gap path order fixes on which side of the block that move occurs. A disjoint move cannot consume one of the same input squares in successive execution. For an exchange of two distinct available blocks or moves, the separating crossing of the rectangle, or separating swap of a prism, orders all dependencies between their redexes. The resulting sorted realization depends only on z and the pair.

Thus each remains available after the other. Put both blocks into the same augmented schedule. If they share a moving polygon, their disjoint consecutive subpaths on its gap route fix their order. Otherwise the same product order and rectangular input check apply. The two distinct negative prism pastes appear in separate stages of this common 3-reading, so their replacements commute by strict interchange. Any two increment paths with the same counts now agree by moving the first required increment forward, then iterating. Parallel local 4-cells have the same w by injectivity of the fourth differential and consequently coincide. There are no strict generators above local four.
